chapter_title: Mr Tulliver, of Dorlcote Mill, Declares His Resolution about Tom
text:
“It seems a bit a pity, though,” said Mr Tulliver, “as the
lad should take after the mother’s side instead o’ the little
wench. That’s the worst on’t wi’ crossing o’ breeds:
you can never justly calkilate what’ll come on’t. The little un
takes after my side, now: she’s twice as ’cute as Tom. Too
’cute for a woman, I’m afraid,” continued Mr Tulliver,
turning his head dubiously first on one side and then on the other.
“It’s no mischief much while she’s a little un; but an
over-’cute woman’s no better nor a long-tailed
sheep,—she’ll fetch none the bigger price for that.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mr. Tulliver introduces Maggie explicitly and contrasts her intelligence with Tom's slowness, revealing his anxieties about a clever daughter and her marriageability—central to the novel's themes.
enrichment.best_quote: an over-'cute woman's no better nor a long-tailed sheep,—she'll fetch none the bigger price for that
enrichment.summary: Mr. Tulliver reflects that his young daughter Maggie is cleverer than Tom but worries that excessive intelligence in a woman is undesirable and will harm her marriage prospects.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver, of Dorlcote Mill, Declares His Resolution about Tom
text:
“Yes, it  is  a mischief while she’s a little un, Mr
Tulliver, for it runs to naughtiness. How to keep her in a clean pinafore two
hours together passes my cunning. An’ now you put me i’
mind,” continued Mrs Tulliver, rising and going to the window, “I
don’t know where she is now, an’ it’s pretty nigh tea-time.
Ah, I thought so,—wanderin’ up an’ down by the water, like a
wild thing: She’ll tumble in some day.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mrs. Tulliver's anxiety about Maggie's naughtiness and her concern about drowning is domestic character work, though it foreshadows the novel's ending.
enrichment.summary: Mrs. Tulliver complains that Maggie is wild and disobedient, constantly wandering by the water despite warnings, and fears she will drown.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver, of Dorlcote Mill, Declares His Resolution about Tom
text:
Mrs Tulliver rapped the window sharply, beckoned, and shook her head,—a
process which she repeated more than once before she returned to her chair.

enrichment.interest_rationale: A brief action line showing Mrs. Tulliver signaling to someone at the window, purely transitional with no significant narrative or thematic content.
enrichment.summary: Mrs. Tulliver raps on the window, beckons, and shakes her head repeatedly before returning to her chair.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver, of Dorlcote Mill, Declares His Resolution about Tom
text:
“You talk o’ ’cuteness, Mr Tulliver,” she observed as
she sat down, “but I’m sure the child’s half an idiot
i’ some things; for if I send her upstairs to fetch anything, she forgets
what she’s gone for, an’ perhaps ’ull sit down on the floor
i’ the sunshine an’ plait her hair an’ sing to herself like a
Bedlam creatur’, all the while I’m waiting for her downstairs. That
niver run i’ my family, thank God! no more nor a brown skin as makes her
look like a mulatter. I don’t like to fly i’ the face o’
Providence, but it seems hard as I should have but one gell, an’ her so
comical.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mrs. Tulliver's detailed complaints about Maggie's absentmindedness and unkempt appearance reveal maternal exasperation and family tension, with hints of self-awareness about Maggie's difference.
enrichment.summary: Mrs. Tulliver criticizes Maggie's forgetfulness, daydreaming, and unkempt appearance, worrying that her dark skin and wild behavior are embarrassing deviations from family norms.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver, of Dorlcote Mill, Declares His Resolution about Tom
text:
“Pooh, nonsense!” said Mr Tulliver; “she’s a straight,
black-eyed wench as anybody need wish to see. I don’t know i’ what
she’s behind other folks’s children; and she can read almost as
well as the parson.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mr. Tulliver's brief defense of Maggie is affectionate but routine, offering minimal narrative or thematic advancement.
enrichment.summary: Mr. Tulliver dismisses his wife's complaints and praises Maggie as a handsome girl who can read well, showing paternal affection.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver, of Dorlcote Mill, Declares His Resolution about Tom
text:
“But her hair won’t curl all I can do with it, and she’s so
franzy about having it put i’ paper, and I’ve such work as never
was to make her stand and have it pinched with th’ irons.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mrs. Tulliver's complaint about Maggie's uncurled hair is trivial domestic concern without thematic or narrative significance.
enrichment.summary: Mrs. Tulliver complains that Maggie's hair will not curl and resists being set in papers.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver, of Dorlcote Mill, Declares His Resolution about Tom
text: “Cut it off—cut it off short,” said the father, rashly.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mr. Tulliver's off-hand suggestion to cut Maggie's hair is a minor plot point but lacks significance on its own.
enrichment.summary: Mr. Tulliver rashly suggests cutting Maggie's hair short to solve the problem.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver, of Dorlcote Mill, Declares His Resolution about Tom
text:
“How can you talk so, Mr Tulliver? She’s too big a gell—gone
nine, and tall of her age—to have her hair cut short; an’
there’s her cousin Lucy’s got a row o’ curls round her head,
an’ not a hair out o’ place. It seems hard as my sister Deane
should have that pretty child; I’m sure Lucy takes more after me nor my
own child does. Maggie, Maggie,” continued the mother, in a tone of
half-coaxing fretfulness, as this small mistake of nature entered the room,
“where’s the use o’ my telling you to keep away from the
water? You’ll tumble in and be drownded some day, an’ then
you’ll be sorry you didn’t do as mother told you.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mrs. Tulliver's shocked response and contrast with Lucy Deane introduces sibling dynamics and Maggie's entrance, marking a transition to the novel's central character with emotional force.
enrichment.best_quote: It seems hard as my sister Deane should have that pretty child; I'm sure Lucy takes more after me nor my own child does
enrichment.summary: Mrs. Tulliver refuses to cut Maggie's hair short and compares her unfavorably to her cousin Lucy, who has perfect curls; Maggie enters the room as her mother fretfully scolds her.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver, of Dorlcote Mill, Declares His Resolution about Tom
text:
Maggie’s hair, as she threw off her bonnet, painfully confirmed her
mother’s accusation. Mrs Tulliver, desiring her daughter to have a
curled crop, “like other folks’s children,” had had it cut
too short in front to be pushed behind the ears; and as it was usually straight
an hour after it had been taken out of paper, Maggie was incessantly tossing
her head to keep the dark, heavy locks out of her gleaming black eyes,—an
action which gave her very much the air of a small Shetland pony.

enrichment.interest_rationale: The vivid physical description of Maggie's appearance and her habitual gesture (tossing her head) creates a memorable first impression and establishes her kinetic energy and defiance.
enrichment.best_quote: an action which gave her very much the air of a small Shetland pony
enrichment.summary: Maggie's short, straight, dark hair and her constant head-tossing gesture to keep it from her eyes give her the appearance of a small Shetland pony.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver, of Dorlcote Mill, Declares His Resolution about Tom
text:
“Oh, dear, oh, dear, Maggie, what are you thinkin’ of, to throw
your bonnet down there? Take it upstairs, there’s a good gell, an’
let your hair be brushed, an’ put your other pinafore on, an’
change your shoes, do, for shame; an’ come an’ go on with your
patchwork, like a little lady.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mrs. Tulliver's imperative to Maggie is routine maternal nagging without thematic or narrative significance.
enrichment.summary: Mrs. Tulliver orders Maggie to pick up her bonnet, brush her hair, change her clothes, and do her patchwork like a proper young lady.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver, of Dorlcote Mill, Declares His Resolution about Tom
text:
“Oh, mother,” said Maggie, in a vehemently cross tone, “I
don’t  want  to do my patchwork.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Maggie's defiant refusal of patchwork establishes her character: intelligent, rebellious, and impatient with feminine convention—a key trait driving her arc.
enrichment.summary: Maggie refuses crossly to do her patchwork, rejecting what her mother views as proper feminine activity.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver, of Dorlcote Mill, Declares His Resolution about Tom
text:
“What! not your pretty patchwork, to make a counterpane for your aunt
Glegg?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mrs. Tulliver's rhetorical question is routine maternal coaxing without significant content.
enrichment.summary: Mrs. Tulliver tries to persuade Maggie by reminding her the patchwork is for her aunt Glegg.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver, of Dorlcote Mill, Declares His Resolution about Tom
text:
“It’s foolish work,” said Maggie, with a toss of her
mane,—“tearing things to pieces to sew ’em together again.
And I don’t want to do anything for my aunt Glegg. I don’t like
her.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Maggie's articulate dismissal of patchwork as futile and her frank expression of dislike for her aunt reveal her sharp intelligence and fearless honesty.
enrichment.best_quote: It's foolish work, tearing things to pieces to sew 'em together again
enrichment.summary: Maggie calls patchwork foolish and frankly states she does not like her aunt Glegg or wish to do anything for her.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver, of Dorlcote Mill, Declares His Resolution about Tom
text:
Exit Maggie, dragging her bonnet by the string, while Mr Tulliver laughs
audibly.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Maggie's exit is a brief action line signaling her departure, with Mr. Tulliver's laughter suggesting paternal approval of her spirit.
enrichment.summary: Maggie exits dragging her bonnet, while Mr. Tulliver laughs at her spirited defiance.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver, of Dorlcote Mill, Declares His Resolution about Tom
text:
“I wonder at you, as you’ll laugh at her, Mr Tulliver,” said
the mother, with feeble fretfulness in her tone. “You encourage her
i’ naughtiness. An’ her aunts will have it as it’s me spoils
her.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mrs. Tulliver's weak protest about Mr. Tulliver's encouragement of Maggie is routine domestic friction.
enrichment.summary: Mrs. Tulliver weakly protests that Mr. Tulliver encourages Maggie's naughtiness and that her family will blame her for it.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver, of Dorlcote Mill, Declares His Resolution about Tom
text:
Mrs Tulliver was what is called a good-tempered person,—never cried,
when she was a baby, on any slighter ground than hunger and pins; and from the
cradle upward had been healthy, fair, plump, and dull-witted; in short, the
flower of her family for beauty and amiability. But milk and mildness are not
the best things for keeping, and when they turn only a little sour, they may
disagree with young stomachs seriously. I have often wondered whether those
early Madonnas of Raphael, with the blond faces and somewhat stupid expression,
kept their placidity undisturbed when their strong-limbed, strong-willed boys
got a little too old to do without clothing. I think they must have been given
to feeble remonstrance, getting more and more peevish as it became more and
more ineffectual.

enrichment.interest_rationale: The narrator's extended analysis of Mrs. Tulliver's character—her bland good nature and how it has soured—offers psychological depth and engages the novel's central tensions around maternal authority and growing conflict.
enrichment.best_quote: milk and mildness are not the best things for keeping, and when they turn only a little sour, they may disagree with young stomachs seriously
enrichment.summary: The narrator reflects that Mrs. Tulliver's lifelong placidity and dullness, while marked by good temper and beauty, have curdled into ineffectual fretfulness when confronted with stronger-willed children.

text:
So Tom went on even to the fifth half-year—till he was turned
sixteen—at King’s Lorton, while Maggie was growing with a rapidity
which her aunts considered highly reprehensible, at Miss Firniss’s
boarding-school in the ancient town of Laceham on the Floss, with cousin Lucy
for her companion. In her early letters to Tom she had always sent her love to
Philip, and asked many questions about him, which were answered by brief
sentences about Tom’s toothache, and a turf-house which he was helping to
build in the garden, with other items of that kind. She was pained to hear Tom
say in the holidays that Philip was as queer as ever again, and often cross.
They were no longer very good friends, she perceived; and when she reminded Tom
that he ought always to love Philip for being so good to him when his foot was
bad, he answered: “Well, it isn’t my fault;  I  don’t do
anything to him.” She hardly ever saw Philip during the remainder of
their school-life; in the Midsummer holidays he was always away at the seaside,
and at Christmas she could only meet him at long intervals in the street of St
Ogg’s. When they did meet, she remembered her promise to kiss him, but,
as a young lady who had been at a boarding-school, she knew now that such a
greeting was out of the question, and Philip would not expect it. The promise
was void, like so many other sweet, illusory promises of our childhood; void as
promises made in Eden before the seasons were divided, and when the starry
blossoms grew side by side with the ripening peach,—impossible to be
fulfilled when the golden gates had been passed.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Establishes Maggie and Tom's separation during schooling and poignantly traces the dissolution of Maggie and Philip's childhood connection through a philosophically resonant metaphor about lost innocence.
enrichment.best_quote: void as promises made in Eden before the seasons were divided, and when the starry blossoms grew side by side with the ripening peach,—impossible to be fulfilled when the golden gates had been passed.
enrichment.summary: Maggie and Tom attend different boarding schools; Maggie's childhood bond with Philip deteriorates as she matures, and she realizes their youthful promise of affection can never be fulfilled in adulthood.

text:
But when their father was actually engaged in the long-threatened lawsuit, and
Wakem, as the agent at once of Pivart and Old Harry, was acting against him,
even Maggie felt, with some sadness, that they were not likely ever to have any
intimacy with Philip again; the very name of Wakem made her father angry, and
she had once heard him say that if that crook-backed son lived to inherit his
father’s ill-gotten gains, there would be a curse upon him. “Have
as little to do with him at school as you can, my lad,” he said to Tom;
and the command was obeyed the more easily because Mr Sterling by this time
had two additional pupils; for though this gentleman’s rise in the world
was not of that meteor-like rapidity which the admirers of his extemporaneous
eloquence had expected for a preacher whose voice demanded so wide a sphere, he
had yet enough of growing prosperity to enable him to increase his expenditure
in continued disproportion to his income.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Provides necessary plot exposition about the lawsuit and explains the enforced separation of Maggie and Philip, with a touch of social commentary on Mr Sterling's pretensions.
enrichment.summary: The Tulliver lawsuit against Pivart proceeds with Wakem acting as agent; Mr Tulliver forbids Tom to associate with Philip, and Mr Sterling increases his pupils despite his extemporaneous preaching never achieving the prominence expected.

text:
As for Tom’s school course, it went on with mill-like monotony, his mind
continuing to move with a slow, half-stifled pulse in a medium of uninteresting
or unintelligible ideas. But each vacation he brought home larger and larger
drawings with the satiny rendering of landscape, and water-colours in vivid
greens, together with manuscript books full of exercises and problems, in which
the handwriting was all the finer because he gave his whole mind to it. Each
vacation he brought home a new book or two, indicating his progress through
different stages of history, Christian doctrine, and Latin literature; and that
passage was not entirely without results, besides the possession of the books.
Tom’s ear and tongue had become accustomed to a great many words and
phrases which are understood to be signs of an educated condition; and though
he had never really applied his mind to any one of his lessons, the lessons had
left a deposit of vague, fragmentary, ineffectual notions. Mr Tulliver, seeing
signs of acquirement beyond the reach of his own criticism, thought it was
probably all right with Tom’s education; he observed, indeed, that there
were no maps, and not enough “summing”; but he made no formal
complaint to Mr Stelling. It was a puzzling business, this schooling; and if he
took Tom away, where could he send him with better effect?

enrichment.interest_rationale: Offers insight into Tom's superficial education and Mr Tulliver's passive acceptance of it, establishing themes of wasted potential and parental blindness.
enrichment.summary: Tom's schooling proceeds with mechanical monotony; despite bringing home drawings and books showing outward progress, his mind has absorbed only fragmentary notions, yet his father remains satisfied with the appearance of education.

text:
By the time Tom had reached his last quarter at King’s Lorton, the years
had made striking changes in him since the day we saw him returning from Mr
Jacobs’s academy. He was a tall youth now, carrying himself without the
least awkwardness, and speaking without more shyness than was a becoming
symptom of blended diffidence and pride; he wore his tail-coat and his stand-up
collars, and watched the down on his lip with eager impatience, looking every
day at his virgin razor, with which he had provided himself in the last
holidays. Philip had already left,—at the autumn quarter,—that he
might go to the south for the winter, for the sake of his health; and this
change helped to give Tom the unsettled, exultant feeling that usually belongs
to the last months before leaving school. This quarter, too, there was some
hope of his father’s lawsuit being decided;  that  made the prospect
of home more entirely pleasurable. For Tom, who had gathered his view of the
case from his father’s conversation, had no doubt that Pivart would be
beaten.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Marks Tom's maturation and approaching adulthood, capturing his vanity and optimism on the eve of catastrophe, heightened by dramatic irony of his false confidence in winning the lawsuit.
enrichment.summary: Tom reaches his final quarter at school as a tall, vain young man eager for adulthood; Philip has left for health reasons, and Tom confidently expects his father to win the lawsuit.

text:
Tom had not heard anything from home for some weeks,—a fact which did not
surprise him, for his father and mother were not apt to manifest their
affection in unnecessary letters,—when, to his great surprise, on the
morning of a dark, cold day near the end of November, he was told, soon after
entering the study at nine o’clock, that his sister was in the
drawing-room. It was Mrs Stelling who had come into the study to tell him, and
she left him to enter the drawing-room alone.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Masterfully builds suspense through atmospheric detail and Tom's bewilderment as his sister appears without warning on a dark November morning, signaling the imminent catastrophe.
enrichment.summary: On a dark November morning, Mrs Stelling surprises Tom by announcing that his sister Maggie has arrived unexpectedly at school.

text:
Maggie, too, was tall now, with braided and coiled hair; she was almost as tall
as Tom, though she was only thirteen; and she really looked older than he did
at that moment. She had thrown off her bonnet, her heavy braids were pushed
back from her forehead, as if it would not bear that extra load, and her young
face had a strangely worn look, as her eyes turned anxiously toward the door.
When Tom entered she did not speak, but only went up to him, put her arms round
his neck, and kissed him earnestly. He was used to various moods of hers, and
felt no alarm at the unusual seriousness of her greeting.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Poignantly portrays Maggie's emotional maturity and worn appearance at thirteen, contrasting her gravity with Tom's innocence, and establishes the emotional intensity of their bond at this pivotal moment.
enrichment.summary: Maggie appears unusually tall and mature for thirteen, her face worn and anxious; she greets Tom with earnest affection rather than words.

text:
“Why, how is it you’re come so early this cold morning, Maggie? Did
you come in the gig?” said Tom, as she backed toward the sofa, and drew
him to her side.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Simple dialogue establishing that Maggie has traveled by coach rather than gig; purely functional exposition with no memorable content.
enrichment.summary: Tom asks why Maggie arrived in the cold morning.

text: “No, I came by the coach. I’ve walked from the turnpike.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Brief factual answer providing travel information; routine connective dialogue with no narrative significance.
enrichment.summary: Maggie states she came by coach and walked from the turnpike.

text:
“But how is it you’re not at school? The holidays have not begun
yet?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Routine question about holiday schedules with no dramatic or thematic content.
enrichment.summary: Tom asks why Maggie is not at school.

text:
“Father wanted me at home,” said Maggie, with a slight trembling of
the lip. “I came home three or four days ago.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Maggie's trembling lip hints at emotional distress and begins the gradual revelation of bad news, but the statement itself is minimally informative.
enrichment.summary: Maggie reveals she came home three or four days ago at her father's request.

text: “Isn’t my father well?” said Tom, rather anxiously.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Tom's anxiety surfaces but his question is straightforward; it builds tension incrementally rather than providing revelation.
enrichment.summary: Tom expresses anxiety about his father's health.

text:
“Not quite,” said Maggie. “He’s very unhappy, Tom. The
lawsuit is ended, and I came to tell you because I thought it would be better
for you to know it before you came home, and I didn’t like only to send
you a letter.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: The pivotal revelation that the lawsuit is lost delivers the central catastrophe of the chapter; Maggie's deliberate choice to tell Tom in person demonstrates her emotional maturity and love.
enrichment.summary: Maggie reveals that the lawsuit has ended and father is unhappy; she came to prepare Tom before he returned home.

text:
“My father hasn’t lost?” said Tom, hastily, springing from
the sofa, and standing before Maggie with his hands suddenly thrust into his
pockets.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Tom's immediate question about financial loss is natural but the dialogue itself is functional without memorable expression.
enrichment.summary: Tom asks if his father has lost the lawsuit.

text: “Yes, dear Tom,” said Maggie, looking up at him with trembling.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Maggie's brief, trembling affirmation confirms the loss but adds little beyond emotional tone.
enrichment.summary: Maggie confirms the lawsuit is lost.

text: Tom was silent a minute or two, with his eyes fixed on the floor. Then he said:

enrichment.interest_rationale: Tom's silent moment of processing the news shows emotional response but provides minimal narrative content.
enrichment.summary: Tom becomes silent and looks at the floor, processing the news.

text: “My father will have to pay a good deal of money, then?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Tom's follow-up question about monetary loss is a logical but unremarkable continuation of the revelation sequence.
enrichment.summary: Tom asks if his father must pay a large amount of money.

text: “Yes,” said Maggie, rather faintly.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Maggie's faint affirmation is purely functional dialogue with minimal content.
enrichment.summary: Maggie confirms the father must pay money.

text:
“Well, it can’t be helped,” said Tom, bravely, not
translating the loss of a large sum of money into any tangible results.
“But my father’s very much vexed, I dare say?” he added,
looking at Maggie, and thinking that her agitated face was only part of her
girlish way of taking things.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Tom attempts brave stoicism but his naïveté about financial consequences and his misreading of Maggie's distress reveal his immaturity in a moment that presages his deeper shock.
enrichment.best_quote: Well, it can't be helped
enrichment.summary: Tom attempts to respond bravely, minimizing the monetary loss, but misinterprets Maggie's agitation as girlish anxiety.

text:
“Yes,” said Maggie, again faintly. Then, urged to fuller speech by
Tom’s freedom from apprehension, she said loudly and rapidly, as if the
words  would  burst from her: “Oh, Tom, he will lose the mill and
the land and everything; he will have nothing left.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: The climactic revelation that the family will lose everything—the mill, the land, all property—transforms Tom's understanding completely; Maggie's urgent emotional outburst is the emotional apex of her burden.
enrichment.best_quote: Oh, Tom, he will lose the mill and the land and everything; he will have nothing left.
enrichment.summary: Maggie urgently reveals that her father will lose the mill, the land, and everything he owns.

text:
Tom’s eyes flashed out one look of surprise at her, before he turned
pale, and trembled visibly. He said nothing, but sat down on the sofa again,
looking vaguely out of the opposite window.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Tom's physical and emotional collapse upon learning of total financial ruin demonstrates the shattering of his worldview and his entry into adulthood through trauma.
enrichment.summary: Tom turns pale and trembles visibly upon learning the full extent of the loss, then sits in stunned silence.

text:
Anxiety about the future had never entered Tom’s mind. His father had
always ridden a good horse, kept a good house, and had the cheerful, confident
air of a man who has plenty of property to fall back upon. Tom had never
dreamed that his father would “fail”;  that  was a form of
misfortune which he had always heard spoken of as a deep disgrace, and disgrace
was an idea that he could not associate with any of his relations, least of all
with his father. A proud sense of family respectability was part of the very
air Tom had been born and brought up in. He knew there were people in St
Ogg’s who made a show without money to support it, and he had always
heard such people spoken of by his own friends with contempt and reprobation.
He had a strong belief, which was a lifelong habit, and required no definite
evidence to rest on, that his father could spend a great deal of money if he
chose; and since his education at Mr Stelling’s had given him a more
expensive view of life, he had often thought that when he got older he would
make a figure in the world, with his horse and dogs and saddle, and other
accoutrements of a fine young man, and show himself equal to any of his
contemporaries at St Ogg’s, who might consider themselves a grade above
him in society because their fathers were professional men, or had large
oil-mills. As to the prognostics and headshaking of his aunts and uncles, they
had never produced the least effect on him, except to make him think that aunts
and uncles were disagreeable society; he had heard them find fault in much the
same way as long as he could remember. His father knew better than they did.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Profound narrative analysis of Tom's innocence and his cultural conditioning regarding respectability, family honor, and social position; his blindness to financial vulnerability is philosophically and thematically rich.
enrichment.best_quote: A proud sense of family respectability was part of the very air Tom had been born and brought up in.
enrichment.summary: The narrator explains how Tom's upbringing in an atmosphere of financial confidence and family respectability has left him unprepared for his father's failure, a concept he associated with deep disgrace.

text:
The down had come on Tom’s lip, yet his thoughts and expectations had
been hitherto only the reproduction, in changed forms, of the boyish dreams in
which he had lived three years ago. He was awakened now with a violent shock.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Crystallizes the moment of Tom's violent awakening from boyish dreams to harsh reality; the metaphor of the down on his lip contrasts physical maturity with psychological naïveté.
enrichment.summary: Despite physical signs of adulthood, Tom's thoughts and expectations have remained boyish until this moment of violent awakening.

text:
Maggie was frightened at Tom’s pale, trembling silence. There was
something else to tell him,—something worse. She threw her arms round him
at last, and said, with a half sob:

enrichment.interest_rationale: Maggie's fear at Tom's silence and her awareness of worse news yet to come sustains the dramatic tension and reaffirms her emotional maturity and burden.
enrichment.summary: Maggie becomes frightened by Tom's continued silence and realizes she still has worse news to tell him.

text:
“Oh, Tom—dear, dear Tom, don’t fret too much; try and bear it
well.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Maggie's tender exhortation to Tom shows her compassion but the dialogue itself is simple emotional appeal without memorable language.
enrichment.summary: Maggie embraces Tom and urges him to bear the news with courage.

text:
Tom turned his cheek passively to meet her entreating kisses, and there
gathered a moisture in his eyes, which he just rubbed away with his hand. The
action seemed to rouse him, for he shook himself and said: “I shall go
home, with you, Maggie. Didn’t my father say I was to go?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Tom's passive acceptance of Maggie's comfort and his emotional suppression—rubbing away tears—contrasts with his growing sense of duty to act; suggests his emerging masculine role in crisis.
enrichment.summary: Tom accepts Maggie's affection silently, quickly moves past sentiment, and insists on going home, believing his father expects him.

text:
“No, Tom, father didn’t wish it,” said Maggie, her anxiety
about  his  feeling helping her to master her agitation. What  would 
he do when she told him all? “But mother wants you to come,—poor
mother!—she cries so. Oh, Tom, it’s very dreadful at home.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Maggie clarifies family expectations while revealing the emotional distress at home; her anxiety about Tom's reaction when told the whole truth demonstrates her awareness of how much worse the situation truly is.
enrichment.summary: Maggie says father did not wish Tom to come but mother wants him home; she hints that things are dreadful at home.

text:
Maggie’s lips grew whiter, and she began to tremble almost as Tom had
done. The two poor things clung closer to each other, both trembling,—the
one at an unshapen fear, the other at the image of a terrible certainty. When
Maggie spoke, it was hardly above a whisper.

enrichment.interest_rationale: The emotional mirror of the two young people trembling—one at undefined fear, one at known tragedy—deepens their bond and emphasizes their shared burden at the threshold of adulthood.
enrichment.summary: Both Maggie and Tom tremble together—Maggie becoming pale, both clinging closer; Maggie can barely speak.

text: “And—and—poor father——”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Maggie's incomplete utterance about their father heightens suspense but contains no independent narrative content.
enrichment.summary: Maggie begins to speak about their father but cannot finish.

text:
Maggie could not utter it. But the suspense was intolerable to Tom. A vague
idea of going to prison, as a consequence of debt, was the shape his fears had
begun to take.

enrichment.interest_rationale: The narrator reveals Tom's fear of imprisonment for debt—a social reality of the period—but the exposition is straightforward without literary distinction.
enrichment.summary: Tom's worst fear shapes itself as the possibility that his father might be imprisoned for debt.

text:
“Where’s my father?” he said impatiently. “ Tell 
me, Maggie.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Tom's impatient demand for the truth is natural but functionally simple dialogue.
enrichment.summary: Tom urgently demands to know where his father is.

text:
“He’s at home,” said Maggie, finding it easier to reply to
that question. “But,” she added, after a pause, “not
himself—he fell off his horse. He has known nobody but me ever
since—he seems to have lost his senses. O father,
father——”

enrichment.interest_rationale: The revelation that Mr Tulliver has suffered a fall from his horse and lost his senses is devastating; it transforms the catastrophe from financial to profoundly personal and tragic, shocking both Tom and the reader.
enrichment.best_quote: He's at home. But he fell off his horse. He has known nobody but me ever since—he seems to have lost his senses.
enrichment.summary: Maggie reveals that Mr Tulliver fell from his horse and has lost consciousness since the accident, recognizing no one but Maggie.

text:
With these last words, Maggie’s sobs burst forth with the more violence
for the previous struggle against them. Tom felt that pressure of the heart
which forbids tears; he had no distinct vision of their troubles as Maggie had,
who had been at home; he only felt the crushing weight of what seemed
unmitigated misfortune. He tightened his arm almost convulsively round Maggie
as she sobbed, but his face looked rigid and tearless, his eyes blank,—as
if a black curtain of cloud had suddenly fallen on his path.

enrichment.interest_rationale: One of the chapter's emotional crescendos: Maggie's sobs break forth after sustained effort, and Tom's rigid, tearless response to crushing misfortune perfectly captures his frozen shock and Maggie's release; profoundly moving portrayal of how trauma manifests differently.
enrichment.best_quote: He tightened his arm almost convulsively round Maggie as she sobbed, but his face looked rigid and tearless, his eyes blank,—as if a black curtain of cloud had suddenly fallen on his path.
enrichment.summary: Maggie's suppressed sobs burst forth violently, while Tom, feeling the crushing weight of misfortune, cannot weep; his face becomes rigid and his eyes blank.

text:
But Maggie soon checked herself abruptly; a single thought had acted on her
like a startling sound.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Maggie's sudden emotional shift from overwhelming grief to practical decision-making shows her resilience but the exposition is straightforward.
enrichment.summary: Maggie abruptly regains composure as a single thought strikes her, redirecting her focus to practical matters.

text:
“We must set out, Tom, we must not stay. Father will miss me; we must be
at the turnpike at ten to meet the coach.” She said this with hasty
decision, rubbing her eyes, and rising to seize her bonnet.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Maggie's urgent decision to return home is character-revealing (duty, responsibility) but expressed in routine dialogue.
enrichment.summary: Maggie insists they must leave immediately to meet the coach at the turnpike, as her father will miss her.

text:
Tom at once felt the same impulse, and rose too. “Wait a minute,
Maggie,” he said. “I must speak to Mr Stelling, and then
we’ll go.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Tom's practical agreement and brief instruction to Maggie is functional dialogue with no narrative interest.
enrichment.summary: Tom agrees to leave but says he must first speak to Mr Stelling.

text:
He thought he must go to the study where the pupils were; but on his way he met
Mr Stelling, who had heard from his wife that Maggie appeared to be in trouble
when she asked for her brother, and now that he thought the brother and sister
had been alone long enough, was coming to inquire and offer his sympathy.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mr Stelling's appearance shows concern and impending kindness, but the narrative exposition is straightforward without particular insight.
enrichment.summary: Mr Stelling encounters Tom in the passage, having learned from his wife that the siblings are in distress.

text:
“Please, sir, I must go home,” Tom said abruptly, as he met Mr
Stelling in the passage. “I must go back with my sister directly. My
father’s lost his lawsuit—he’s lost all his
property—and he’s very ill.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Tom's abrupt, emotional explanation to Mr Stelling consolidates all bad news in one powerful statement; his directness conveys both shock and new-found sense of responsibility.
enrichment.best_quote: My father's lost his lawsuit—he's lost all his property—and he's very ill.
enrichment.summary: Tom urgently tells Mr Stelling that he must leave school immediately because his father has lost the lawsuit, all property, and is very ill.

text:
Mr Stelling felt like a kind-hearted man; he foresaw a probable money loss for
himself, but this had no appreciable share in his feeling, while he looked with
grave pity at the brother and sister for whom youth and sorrow had begun
together. When he knew how Maggie had come, and how eager she was to get home
again, he hurried their departure, only whispering something to Mrs Stelling,
who had followed him, and who immediately left the room.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mr Stelling's kindly, swift action demonstrates human goodness in crisis; the narrator's brief comment about his initial concern for money loss reveals his eventual triumph of human sympathy over self-interest.
enrichment.summary: Mr Stelling, though concerned about potential monetary loss, is moved by pity for the siblings and hastens their departure after learning how eager Maggie is to get home.

text:
Tom and Maggie were standing on the door-step, ready to set out, when Mrs
Stelling came with a little basket, which she hung on Maggie’s arm,
saying: “Do remember to eat something on the way, dear.”
Maggie’s heart went out toward this woman whom she had never liked, and
she kissed her silently. It was the first sign within the poor child of that
new sense which is the gift of sorrow,—that susceptibility to the bare
offices of humanity which raises them into a bond of loving fellowship, as to
haggard men among the ice-bergs the mere presence of an ordinary comrade stirs
the deep fountains of affection.

enrichment.interest_rationale: A poignant moment of grace: Maggie's sudden affection for Mrs Stelling demonstrates the narrator's profound insight into how sorrow awakens compassion; the metaphor of ice-bergs and human warmth is philosophically rich and emotionally moving.
enrichment.best_quote: It was the first sign within the poor child of that new sense which is the gift of sorrow,—that susceptibility to the bare offices of humanity which raises them into a bond of loving fellowship, as to haggard men among the ice-bergs the mere presence of an ordinary comrade stirs the deep fountains of affection.
enrichment.summary: Mrs Stelling gives Maggie a basket of food; Maggie, who never liked her before, kisses her silently—a moment showing how sorrow awakens susceptibility to human kindness.

text:
Mr Stelling put his hand on Tom’s shoulder and said: “God bless
you, my boy; let me know how you get on.” Then he pressed Maggie’s
hand; but there were no audible good-byes. Tom had so often thought how joyful
he should be the day he left school “for good”! And now his school
years seemed like a holiday that had come to an end.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mr Stelling's blessing and the siblings' departure create a poignant moment; the narrator's ironic reflection on Tom's anticipated joy about leaving school contrasts sharply with the tragic reality of his departure.
enrichment.best_quote: God bless you, my boy; let me know how you get on.
enrichment.summary: Mr Stelling blesses Tom and shakes hands silently with Maggie; the narrator notes Tom had often imagined joyfully leaving school "for good," but it now seems his school years were merely a holiday.

text:
The two slight youthful figures soon grew indistinct on the distant
road,—were soon lost behind the projecting hedgerow.

enrichment.interest_rationale: The image of the two young figures disappearing into the distance is visually poignant and symbolically marks their departure from the safety and innocence of the school world.
enrichment.summary: Tom and Maggie walk away down the road and disappear from sight behind a hedgerow.

text:
They had gone forth together into their life of sorrow, and they would never
more see the sunshine undimmed by remembered cares. They had entered the thorny
wilderness, and the golden gates of their childhood had forever closed behind
them.

enrichment.interest_rationale: The chapter's philosophical and emotional apex: a magnificent summary statement that the siblings have crossed the threshold from childhood innocence to a life of sorrow; the image of closed golden gates perfectly echoes the chapter's opening metaphor, achieving profound thematic closure.
enrichment.best_quote: They had gone forth together into their life of sorrow, and they would never more see the sunshine undimmed by remembered cares. They had entered the thorny wilderness, and the golden gates of their childhood had forever closed behind them.
enrichment.summary: The narrator concludes that the siblings have entered a life of sorrow with their innocence forever lost; the golden gates of childhood have closed behind them permanently.

text:
When Mr Tulliver first knew the fact that the lawsuit was decided against him,
and that Pivart and Wakem were triumphant, every one who happened to observe
him at the time thought that, for so confident and hot-tempered a man, he bore
the blow remarkably well. He thought so himself; he thought he was going to
show that if Wakem or anybody else considered him crushed, they would find
themselves mistaken. He could not refuse to see that the costs of this
protracted suit would take more than he possessed to pay them; but he appeared
to himself to be full of expedients by which he could ward off any results but
such as were tolerable, and could avoid the appearance of breaking down in the
world. All the obstinacy and defiance of his nature, driven out of their old
channel, found a vent for themselves in the immediate formation of plans by
which he would meet his difficulties, and remain Mr Tulliver of Dorlcote Mill
in spite of them. There was such a rush of projects in his brain, that it was
no wonder his face was flushed when he came away from his talk with his
attorney, Mr Gore, and mounted his horse to ride home from Lindum. There was
Furley, who held the mortgage on the land,—a reasonable fellow, who would
see his own interest, Mr Tulliver was convinced, and who would be glad not
only to purchase the whole estate, including the mill and homestead, but would
accept Mr Tulliver as tenant, and be willing to advance money to be repaid
with high interest out of the profits of the business, which would be made over
to him, Mr Tulliver only taking enough barely to maintain himself and his
family. Who would neglect such a profitable investment? Certainly not Furley,
for Mr Tulliver had determined that Furley should meet his plans with the
utmost alacrity; and there are men whose brains have not yet been dangerously
heated by the loss of a lawsuit, who are apt to see in their own interest or
desires a motive for other men’s actions. There was no doubt (in the
miller’s mind) that Furley would do just what was desirable; and if he
did—why, things would not be so very much worse. Mr Tulliver and his
family must live more meagrely and humbly, but it would only be till the
profits of the business had paid off Furley’s advances, and that might be
while Mr Tulliver had still a good many years of life before him. It was clear
that the costs of the suit could be paid without his being obliged to turn out
of his old place, and look like a ruined man. It was certainly an awkward
moment in his affairs. There was that suretyship for poor Riley, who had died
suddenly last April, and left his friend saddled with a debt of two hundred and
fifty pounds,—a fact which had helped to make Mr Tulliver’s
banking book less pleasant reading than a man might desire toward Christmas.
Well! he had never been one of those poor-spirited sneaks who would refuse to
give a helping hand to a fellow-traveller in this puzzling world. The really
vexatious business was the fact that some months ago the creditor who had lent
him the five hundred pounds to repay Mrs Glegg had become uneasy about his
money (set on by Wakem, of course), and Mr Tulliver, still confident that he
should gain his suit, and finding it eminently inconvenient to raise the said
sum until that desirable issue had taken place, had rashly acceded to the
demand that he should give a bill of sale on his household furniture and some
other effects, as security in lieu of the bond. It was all one, he had said to
himself; he should soon pay off the money, and there was no harm in giving that
security any more than another. But now the consequences of this bill of sale
occurred to him in a new light, and he remembered that the time was close at
hand when it would be enforced unless the money were repaid. Two months ago he
would have declared stoutly that he would never be beholden to his wife’s
friends; but now he told himself as stoutly that it was nothing but right and
natural that Bessy should go to the Pullets and explain the thing to them; they
would hardly let Bessy’s furniture be sold, and it might be security to
Pullet if he advanced the money,—there would, after all, be no gift or
favour in the matter. Mr Tulliver would never have asked for anything from so
poor-spirited a fellow for himself, but Bessy might do so if she liked.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Introduces the crucial plot turning point—the lawsuit's loss—and establishes Mr. Tulliver's delusional coping mechanism that will drive the chapter's tragedy.
enrichment.summary: Mr. Tulliver learns his lawsuit is lost but outwardly appears composed, constructing elaborate mental plans to avoid ruin through schemes involving mortgages and advances—deluding himself about Furley's cooperation.

text:
It is precisely the proudest and most obstinate men who are the most liable to
shift their position and contradict themselves in this sudden manner;
everything is easier to them than to face the simple fact that they have been
thoroughly defeated, and must begin life anew. And Mr Tulliver, you perceive,
though nothing more than a superior miller and maltster, was as proud and
obstinate as if he had been a very lofty personage, in whom such dispositions
might be a source of that conspicuous, far-echoing tragedy, which sweeps the
stage in regal robes, and makes the dullest chronicler sublime. The pride and
obstinacy of millers and other insignificant people, whom you pass unnoticingly
on the road every day, have their tragedy too; but it is of that unwept, hidden
sort that goes on from generation to generation, and leaves no
record,—such tragedy, perhaps, as lies in the conflicts of young souls,
hungry for joy, under a lot made suddenly hard to them, under the dreariness of
a home where the morning brings no promise with it, and where the unexpectant
discontent of worn and disappointed parents weighs on the children like a damp,
thick air, in which all the functions of life are depressed; or such tragedy as
lies in the slow or sudden death that follows on a bruised passion, though it
may be a death that finds only a parish funeral. There are certain animals to
which tenacity of position is a law of life,—they can never flourish
again, after a single wrench: and there are certain human beings to whom
predominance is a law of life,—they can only sustain humiliation so long
as they can refuse to believe in it, and, in their own conception, predominate
still.

enrichment.interest_rationale: A remarkable authorial intrusion offering philosophical commentary on pride, obstinacy, and the hidden tragedy of ordinary lives—quintessentially Eliot.
enrichment.best_quote: The pride and obstinacy of millers and other insignificant people, whom you pass unnoticingly on the road every day, have their tragedy too; but it is of that unwept, hidden sort that goes on from generation to generation, and leaves no record
enrichment.summary: The narrator philosophizes on how the proud and obstinate are driven to self-contradiction when facing defeat, and how ordinary people's tragedies—unlike regal tragedies—are hidden and unrecorded.

text:
Mr Tulliver was still predominating, in his own imagination, as he approached
St Ogg’s, through which he had to pass on his way homeward. But what was
it that suggested to him, as he saw the Laceham coach entering the town, to
follow it to the coach-office, and get the clerk there to write a letter,
requiring Maggie to come home the very next day? Mr Tulliver’s own hand
shook too much under his excitement for him to write himself, and he wanted the
letter to be given to the coachman to deliver at Miss Firniss’s school in
the morning. There was a craving which he would not account for to himself, to
have Maggie near him, without delay,—she must come back by the coach
to-morrow.

enrichment.interest_rationale: A turning point: Mr. Tulliver's impulsive decision to summon Maggie reveals both his emotional state and foreshadows his imminent collapse.
enrichment.summary: As Mr. Tulliver approaches St Ogg's, he suddenly arranges for a letter to be written summoning Maggie home immediately, driven by an inexplicable craving for her presence.

text:
To Mrs Tulliver, when he got home, he would admit no difficulties, and scolded
down her burst of grief on hearing that the lawsuit was lost, by angry
assertions that there was nothing to grieve about. He said nothing to her that
night about the bill of sale and the application to Mrs Pullet, for he had
kept her in ignorance of the nature of that transaction, and had explained the
necessity for taking an inventory of the goods as a matter connected with his
will. The possession of a wife conspicuously one’s inferior in intellect
is, like other high privileges, attended with a few inconveniences, and, among
the rest, with the occasional necessity for using a little deception.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Establishes Mr. Tulliver's control of information and deception toward his wife; shows the narrator's sardonic view of marital dynamics.
enrichment.best_quote: The possession of a wife conspicuously one's inferior in intellect is, like other high privileges, attended with a few inconveniences, and, among the rest, with the occasional necessity for using a little deception.
enrichment.summary: Mr. Tulliver hides the details of his financial crisis from Mrs. Tulliver, dismissing her grief and keeping her ignorant of the bill of sale.

text:
The next day Mr Tulliver was again on horseback in the afternoon, on his way
to Mr Gore’s office at St Ogg’s. Gore was to have seen Furley in
the morning, and to have sounded him in relation to Mr Tulliver’s
affairs. But he had not gone half-way when he met a clerk from Mr Gore’s
office, who was bringing a letter to Mr Tulliver. Mr Gore had been prevented
by a sudden call of business from waiting at his office to see Mr Tulliver,
according to appointment, but would be at his office at eleven to-morrow
morning, and meanwhile had sent some important information by letter.

enrichment.interest_rationale: A routine plot mechanism advancing toward the revelation; establishes Mr. Gore's attempt to convey important information.
enrichment.summary: Mr. Tulliver is riding toward Mr. Gore's office when he encounters a clerk delivering a letter from Gore, who was prevented from keeping their appointment.

text:
“Oh!” said Mr Tulliver, taking the letter, but not opening it.
“Then tell Gore I’ll see him to-morrow at eleven”; and he
turned his horse.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Routine dialogue; Mr. Tulliver's response is perfunctory and moves the plot forward mechanically.
enrichment.summary: Mr. Tulliver instructs the clerk to tell Gore he will meet him tomorrow at eleven and turns his horse.

text:
The clerk, struck with Mr Tulliver’s glistening, excited glance, looked
after him for a few moments, and then rode away. The reading of a letter was
not the affair of an instant to Mr Tulliver; he took in the sense of a
statement very slowly through the medium of written or even printed characters;
so he had put the letter in his pocket, thinking he would open it in his
armchair at home. But by-and-by it occurred to him that there might be
something in the letter Mrs Tulliver must not know about, and if so, it would
be better to keep it out of her sight altogether. He stopped his horse, took
out the letter, and read it. It was only a short letter; the substance was,
that Mr Gore had ascertained, on secret, but sure authority, that Furley had
been lately much straitened for money, and had parted with his
securities,—among the rest, the mortgage on Mr Tulliver’s
property, which he had transferred to——Wakem.

enrichment.interest_rationale: The catastrophic revelation: Wakem has acquired the mortgage. This paragraph depicts the lethal moment when Mr. Tulliver's delusions crash into reality, precipitating his stroke.
enrichment.best_quote: Wakem.
enrichment.summary: Mr. Tulliver reads Gore's letter, which reveals that Furley's mortgage on the property has been transferred to Wakem—the very man Mr. Tulliver believed defeated.

text:
In half an hour after this Mr Tulliver’s own wagoner found him lying by
the roadside insensible, with an open letter near him, and his gray horse
snuffing uneasily about him.

enrichment.interest_rationale: The physical consequence of Mr. Tulliver's psychological collapse; the stroke marks the novel's central catastrophe and shifts the narrative focus to Maggie.
enrichment.summary: Mr. Tulliver is found insensible on the roadside by his wagoner, the open letter beside him.

text:
When Maggie reached home that evening, in obedience to her father’s call,
he was no longer insensible. About an hour before he had become conscious, and
after vague, vacant looks around him, had muttered something about “a
letter,” which he presently repeated impatiently. At the instance of Mr
Turnbull, the medical man, Gore’s letter was brought and laid on the bed,
and the previous impatience seemed to be allayed. The stricken man lay for some
time with his eyes fixed on the letter, as if he were trying to knit up his
thoughts by its help. But presently a new wave of memory seemed to have come
and swept the other away; he turned his eyes from the letter to the door, and
after looking uneasily, as if striving to see something his eyes were too dim
for, he said, “The little wench.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Depicts Mr. Tulliver's regaining consciousness and his urgent, singular focus on Maggie—a touching revelation of his paternal love amid catastrophe.
enrichment.summary: When Maggie arrives home, she finds her father conscious but confused and fixated on seeing 'the little wench'—his term for her.

text:
He repeated the words impatiently from time to time, appearing entirely
unconscious of everything except this one importunate want, and giving no sign
of knowing his wife or any one else; and poor Mrs Tulliver, her feeble
faculties almost paralyzed by this sudden accumulation of troubles, went
backward and forward to the gate to see if the Laceham coach were coming,
though it was not yet time.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Routine exposition of Mrs. Tulliver's distracted anxiety; characterizes her feebleness in crisis.
enrichment.summary: Mr. Tulliver repeats his call for Maggie while Mrs. Tulliver, overwhelmed, anxiously waits by the gate for the coach.

text:
But it came at last, and set down the poor anxious girl, no longer the
“little wench,” except to her father’s fond memory.

enrichment.interest_rationale: A brief, poignant transition marking Maggie's arrival; the phrase 'no longer the little wench, except to her father's fond memory' is reflective but the paragraph itself is minimal.
enrichment.summary: The Laceham coach arrives and sets down Maggie, grown beyond the 'little wench' except in her father's memory.

text:
“Oh, mother, what is the matter?” Maggie said, with pale lips, as
her mother came toward her crying. She didn’t think her father was ill,
because the letter had come at his dictation from the office at St
Ogg’s.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Maggie's alarmed question to her mother; routine emotional reaction to crisis.
enrichment.summary: Maggie asks her weeping mother what the matter is, confused because her father's letter seemed to come from his dictation.

text:
But Mr Turnbull came now to meet her; a medical man is the good angel of the
troubled house, and Maggie ran toward the kind old friend, whom she remembered
as long as she could remember anything, with a trembling, questioning look.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Brief characterization of Mr. Turnbull as a benevolent figure and Maggie's trusted elder; establishes emotional tone for her confrontation with her father's illness.
enrichment.best_quote: a medical man is the good angel of the troubled house
enrichment.summary: Mr. Turnbull comes to meet Maggie, his longtime kindness prompting her to rush toward him with a questioning look.

text:
“Don’t alarm yourself too much, my dear,” he said, taking her
hand. “Your father has had a sudden attack, and has not quite recovered
his memory. But he has been asking for you, and it will do him good to see you.
Keep as quiet as you can; take off your things, and come upstairs with
me.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mr. Turnbull's reassuring but cryptic instructions to Maggie; routine plot mechanism to move her toward her father's room.
enrichment.summary: Mr. Turnbull tells Maggie not to alarm herself, explains her father has had a sudden attack and has been asking for her, and instructs her to stay quiet and come upstairs.

text:
Maggie obeyed, with that terrible beating of the heart which makes existence
seem simply a painful pulsation. The very quietness with which Mr Turnbull
spoke had frightened her susceptible imagination. Her father’s eyes were
still turned uneasily toward the door when she entered and met the strange,
yearning, helpless look that had been seeking her in vain. With a sudden flash
and movement, he raised himself in the bed; she rushed toward him, and clasped
him with agonised kisses.

enrichment.interest_rationale: A poignant scene of reunion: Maggie's emotional terror and her father's yearning recognition culminate in an embrace charged with desperate tenderness.
enrichment.best_quote: she rushed toward him, and clasped him with agonised kisses
enrichment.summary: Maggie enters her father's room with a painful heartbeat; he raises himself in bed upon seeing her and she rushes to embrace him with desperate kisses.

text:
Poor child! it was very early for her to know one of those supreme moments in
life when all we have hoped or delighted in, all we can dread or endure, falls
away from our regard as insignificant; is lost, like a trivial memory, in that
simple, primitive love which knits us to the beings who have been nearest to
us, in their times of helplessness or of anguish.

enrichment.interest_rationale: A transcendent authorial meditation on how supreme moments of crisis strip away all worldly concern and reveal the primitive power of familial love—one of the novel's most luminous passages.
enrichment.best_quote: that simple, primitive love which knits us to the beings who have been nearest to us, in their times of helplessness or of anguish
enrichment.summary: The narrator reflects on how Maggie's supreme moment—seeing her father's helplessness—dissolves all other concerns into a single primitive devotion.

text:
But that flash of recognition had been too great a strain on the father’s
bruised, enfeebled powers. He sank back again in renewed insensibility and
rigidity, which lasted for many hours, and was only broken by a flickering
return of consciousness, in which he took passively everything that was given
to him, and seemed to have a sort of infantine satisfaction in Maggie’s
near presence,—such satisfaction as a baby has when it is returned to the
nurse’s lap.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Depicts Mr. Tulliver's relapse into insensibility and his infantile dependence on Maggie; establishes the permanent nature of his disability.
enrichment.summary: Mr. Tulliver sinks back into insensibility, able only to take comfort from Maggie's presence with an infant-like satisfaction.

text:
Mrs Tulliver sent for her sisters, and there was much wailing and lifting up
of hands below stairs. Both uncles and aunts saw that the ruin of Bessy and her
family was as complete as they had ever foreboded it, and there was a general
family sense that a judgment had fallen on Mr Tulliver, which it would be an
impiety to counteract by too much kindness. But Maggie heard little of this,
scarcely ever leaving her father’s bedside, where she sat opposite him
with her hand on his. Mrs Tulliver wanted to have Tom fetched home, and seemed
to be thinking more of her boy even than of her husband; but the aunts and
uncles opposed this. Tom was better at school, since Mr Turnbull said there
was no immediate danger, he believed. But at the end of the second day, when
Maggie had become more accustomed to her father’s fits of insensibility,
and to the expectation that he would revive from them, the thought of Tom had
become urgent with  her  too; and when her mother sate crying at night and
saying, “My poor lad—it’s nothing but right he should come
home,” Maggie said, “Let me go for him, and tell him, mother;
I’ll go to-morrow morning if father doesn’t know me and want me. It
would be so hard for Tom to come home and not know anything about it
beforehand.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Reveals the family's hypocritical response to ruin as divine judgment, establishes Maggie's self-sacrificial devotion, and introduces the question of fetching Tom home.
enrichment.best_quote: there was a general family sense that a judgment had fallen on Mr Tulliver, which it would be an impiety to counteract by too much kindness
enrichment.summary: The aunts and uncles regard Mr. Tulliver's ruin as divine judgment and offer little kindness; Maggie remains steadfast at her father's side while the family debates whether to fetch Tom home.

text:
And the next morning Maggie went, as we have seen. Sitting on the coach on
their way home, the brother and sister talked to each other in sad, interrupted
whispers.

enrichment.interest_rationale: A brief narrative transition indicating Maggie's journey to fetch Tom; sets up the sibling conversation to follow.
enrichment.summary: Maggie travels by coach the next morning to bring Tom home, and brother and sister speak softly together during the journey.

text:
“They say Mr Wakem has got a mortgage or something on the land,
Tom,” said Maggie. “It was the letter with that news in it that
made father ill, they think.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Maggie informs Tom of the cause of their father's illness; routine expository dialogue.
enrichment.summary: Maggie tells Tom that Wakem has obtained a mortgage on their father's land and that learning this news caused his illness.

text:
“I believe that scoundrel’s been planning all along to ruin my

text:
When the coach set down Tom and Maggie, it was five hours since she had started
from home, and she was thinking with some trembling that her father had perhaps
missed her, and asked for “the little wench” in vain. She thought
of no other change that might have happened.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Routine exposition establishing Maggie's return home and her innocent expectations.
enrichment.summary: Maggie and Tom return home after five hours; Maggie worries her father may have missed her.

chapter_title: Mrs Tulliver’s Teraphim, or Household Gods
text:
She hurried along the gravel-walk and entered the house before Tom; but in the
entrance she was startled by a strong smell of tobacco. The parlour door was
ajar; that was where the smell came from. It was very strange; could any
visitor be smoking at a time like this? Was her mother there? If so, she must
be told that Tom was come. Maggie, after this pause of surprise, was only in
the act of opening the door when Tom came up, and they both looked into the
parlour together.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Creates mystery and unease through sensory detail (tobacco smell) that signals something is wrong.
enrichment.summary: Maggie notices an unusual smell of tobacco in the parlour and puzzles over who the visitor might be.

chapter_title: Mrs Tulliver’s Teraphim, or Household Gods
text:
There was a coarse, dingy man, of whose face Tom had some vague recollection,
sitting in his father’s chair, smoking, with a jug and glass beside him.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Simple descriptive sentence introducing the bailiff; necessary but uneventful.

chapter_title: Mrs Tulliver’s Teraphim, or Household Gods
text:
The truth flashed on Tom’s mind in an instant. To “have the bailiff
in the house,” and “to be sold up,” were phrases which he had
been used to, even as a little boy; they were part of the disgrace and misery
of “failing,” of losing all one’s money, and being
ruined,—sinking into the condition of poor working people. It seemed only
natural this should happen, since his father had lost all his property, and he
thought of no more special cause for this particular form of misfortune than
the loss of the lawsuit. But the immediate presence of this disgrace was so
much keener an experience to Tom than the worst form of apprehension, that he
felt at this moment as if his real trouble had only just begun: it was a touch
on the irritated nerve compared with its spontaneous dull aching.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Significant moment of recognition: Tom understands the full meaning of financial ruin and its social shame.
enrichment.best_quote: sinking into the condition of poor working people
enrichment.summary: Tom instantly grasps that a bailiff in the house means his father has lost everything and the family faces ruin and social disgrace.

chapter_title: Mrs Tulliver’s Teraphim, or Household Gods
text:
“How do you do, sir?” said the man, taking the pipe out of his
mouth, with rough, embarrassed civility. The two young startled faces made him
a little uncomfortable.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Brief, functional dialogue from the bailiff; connective prose.
enrichment.summary: The bailiff greets Tom and Maggie awkwardly.

chapter_title: Mrs Tulliver’s Teraphim, or Household Gods
text:
But Tom turned away hastily without speaking; the sight was too hateful. Maggie
had not understood the appearance of this stranger, as Tom had. She followed
him, whispering: “Who can it be, Tom? What is the matter?” Then,
with a sudden undefined dread lest this stranger might have something to do
with a change in her father, she rushed upstairs, checking herself at the
bedroom door to throw off her bonnet, and enter on tiptoe. All was silent
there; her father was lying, heedless of everything around him, with his eyes
closed as when she had left him. A servant was there, but not her mother.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Develops tension through Maggie's confusion and her anxious search for her mother; reveals Mr Tulliver's deteriorated state.
enrichment.summary: Tom flees in disgust while Maggie rushes upstairs to check on her father, finding him silent and her mother absent.

text:
Mrs Tulliver was not downstairs, not in any of the bedrooms. There was but one
room below the attic which Maggie had left unsearched; it was the storeroom,
where her mother kept all her linen and all the precious “best
things” that were only unwrapped and brought out on special occasions.

enrichment.summary: The only unsearched room is the storeroom where Mrs Tulliver keeps her linens and precious household items.

Tom, preceding Maggie, as they returned along the passage, opened the door of
