chapter_title: An Item Added to the Family Register
text:
That first moment of renunciation and submission was followed by days of
violent struggle in the miller’s mind, as the gradual access of bodily
strength brought with it increasing ability to embrace in one view all the
conflicting conditions under which he found himself. Feeble limbs easily resign
themselves to be tethered, and when we are subdued by sickness it seems
possible to us to fulfil pledges which the old vigor comes back and breaks.
There were times when poor Tulliver thought the fulfilment of his promise to
Bessy was something quite too hard for human nature; he had promised her
without knowing what she was going to say,—she might as well have asked
him to carry a ton weight on his back. But again, there were many feelings
arguing on her side, besides the sense that life had been made hard to her by
having married him. He saw a possibility, by much pinching, of saving money out
of his salary toward paying a second dividend to his creditors, and it would
not be easy elsewhere to get a situation such as he could fill.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Introduces the central internal conflict of the chapter—Tulliver's struggle between bodily weakness that enabled his promise to Bessy and returning strength that makes fulfillment seem impossible.
enrichment.best_quote: Feeble limbs easily resign themselves to be tethered, and when we are subdued by sickness it seems possible to us to fulfil pledges which the old vigor comes back and breaks.
enrichment.summary: Following his initial promise to Bessy to stay at the mill and work under Wakem, Tulliver experiences violent internal struggle as his health returns and he grapples with the difficulty of honoring his pledge.

chapter_title: An Item Added to the Family Register
text:
He had led an easy life, ordering much and working little, and had no aptitude
for any new business. He must perhaps take to day-labour, and his wife must
have help from her sisters,—a prospect doubly bitter to him, now they had
let all Bessy’s precious things be sold, probably because they liked to
set her against him, by making her feel that he had brought her to that pass.
He listened to their admonitory talk, when they came to urge on him what he was
bound to do for poor Bessy’s sake, with averted eyes, that every now and
then flashed on them furtively when their backs were turned. Nothing but the
dread of needing their help could have made it an easier alternative to take
their advice.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Develops Tulliver's grievances and humiliation, showing how dependence on his wife's sisters compounds his shame, but is largely expository.
enrichment.summary: Tulliver's options are all bitter: day-labour would require help from his wife's sisters, whom he resents for allowing Bessy's possessions to be sold and for their moralizing.

chapter_title: An Item Added to the Family Register
text:
But the strongest influence of all was the love of the old premises where he
had run about when he was a boy, just as Tom had done after him. The Tullivers
had lived on this spot for generations, and he had sat listening on a low stool
on winter evenings while his father talked of the old half-timbered mill that
had been there before the last great floods which damaged it so that his
grandfather pulled it down and built the new one. It was when he got able to
walk about and look at all the old objects that he felt the strain of his
clinging affection for the old home as part of his life, part of himself. He
couldn’t bear to think of himself living on any other spot than this,
where he knew the sound of every gate door, and felt that the shape and colour
of every roof and weather-stain and broken hillock was good, because his
growing senses had been fed on them. Our instructed vagrancy, which has hardly
time to linger by the hedgerows, but runs away early to the tropics, and is at
home with palms and banyans,—which is nourished on books of travel and
stretches the theatre of its imagination to the Zambesi,—can hardly get a
dim notion of what an old-fashioned man like Tulliver felt for this spot, where
all his memories centred, and where life seemed like a familiar smooth-handled
tool that the fingers clutch with loving ease. And just now he was living in
that freshened memory of the far-off time which comes to us in the passive
hours of recovery from sickness.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Magnificent passage on Tulliver's deep emotional attachment to place, family history, and memory; includes Eliot's direct commentary on provincial identity versus cosmopolitan vagrancy.
enrichment.best_quote: he felt that the shape and colour of every roof and weather-stain and broken hillock was good, because his growing senses had been fed on them
enrichment.summary: The narrator reflects on Tulliver's profound attachment to the mill and its grounds, rooted in generations of family history and childhood memories, which now strengthens his resolve to remain despite hardship.

chapter_title: An Item Added to the Family Register
text:
“Ay, Luke,” he said one afternoon, as he stood looking over the
orchard gate, “I remember the day they planted those apple-trees. My
father was a huge man for planting,—it was like a merry-making to him to
get a cart full o’ young trees; and I used to stand i’ the cold
with him, and follow him about like a dog.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: A brief dialogue moment establishing Tulliver's nostalgic mood through conversation with Luke, but relatively minor in narrative weight.
enrichment.summary: Tulliver reminisces with Luke about his father planting apple trees in the orchard and how he would follow him about as a child.

chapter_title: An Item Added to the Family Register
text:
Then he turned round, and leaning against the gate-post, looked at the opposite
buildings.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Purely transitional action with no substantive content.
enrichment.summary: Tulliver turns and leans against the gate-post, looking at the opposite buildings.

chapter_title: An Item Added to the Family Register
text:
“The old mill ’ud miss me, I think, Luke. There’s a story as
when the mill changes hands, the river’s angry; I’ve heard my
father say it many a time. There’s no telling whether there mayn’t
be summat  in  the story, for this is a puzzling world, and Old
Harry’s got a finger in it—it’s been too many for me, I
know.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Reveals Tulliver's superstitious beliefs and fatalism; echoes the novel's concern with destiny and the irrational forces that govern his life, foreshadowing later supernatural elements.
enrichment.best_quote: The old mill 'ud miss me, I think, Luke. There's a story as when the mill changes hands, the river's angry
enrichment.summary: Tulliver tells Luke of a folk belief that the river becomes angry when the mill changes hands, suggesting the world is governed by forces beyond human understanding.

chapter_title: An Item Added to the Family Register
text:
“Ay, sir,” said Luke, with soothing sympathy, “what wi’
the rust on the wheat, an’ the firin’ o’ the ricks an’
that, as I’ve seen i’ my time,—things often looks comical;
there’s the bacon fat wi’ our last pig run away like
butter,—it leaves nought but a scratchin’.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Luke's sympathetic response confirms his loyalty but contributes little to plot or character development; provides comic country dialect with mundane examples.
enrichment.summary: Luke agrees sympathetically that strange things happen in the world, offering rural examples of unexplained misfortunes.

chapter_title: An Item Added to the Family Register
text:
“It’s just as if it was yesterday, now,” Mr Tulliver went
on, “when my father began the malting. I remember, the day they finished
the malt-house, I thought summat great was to come of it; for we’d a
plum-pudding that day and a bit of a feast, and I said to my mother,—she
was a fine dark-eyed woman, my mother was,—the little wench ’ull be
as like her as two peas.” Here Mr Tulliver put his stick between his
legs, and took out his snuff-box, for the greater enjoyment of this anecdote,
which dropped from him in fragments, as if he every other moment lost narration
in vision. “I was a little chap no higher much than my mother’s
knee,—she was sore fond of us children, Gritty and me,—and so I
said to her, ‘Mother,’ I said, ‘shall we have plum-pudding
 every  day because o’ the malt-house? She used to tell me o’
that till her dying day. She was but a young woman when she died, my mother
was. But it’s forty good year since they finished the malt-house, and it
isn’t many days out of ’em all as I haven’t looked out into
the yard there, the first thing in the morning,—all weathers, from
year’s end to year’s end. I should go off my head in a new place. I
should be like as if I’d lost my way. It’s all hard, whichever way
I look at it,—the harness ’ull gall me, but it ’ud be summat
to draw along the old road, instead of a new un.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Powerful, character-defining soliloquy in which Tulliver reflects on his family history, his mother's memory, and forty years of attachment to the mill; deeply emotional and quotable.
enrichment.best_quote: It's all hard, whichever way I look at it,—the harness 'ull gall me, but it 'ud be summat to draw along the old road, instead of a new un.
enrichment.summary: Tulliver reminisces about his father's malting enterprise, his mother's beauty and affection, and his forty years of daily life at the mill, concluding that moving elsewhere would destroy him entirely.

chapter_title: An Item Added to the Family Register
text:
“Ay, sir,” said Luke, “you’d be a deal better here nor
in some new place. I can’t abide new places mysen: things is allays
awk’ard,—narrow-wheeled waggins, belike, and the stiles all another
sort, an’ oat-cake i’ some places, tow’rt th’ head
o’ the Floss, there. It’s poor work, changing your
country-side.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Luke's sympathetic echo of Tulliver's sentiments adds local color and reinforces the theme of provincial rootedness, but offers little new information.
enrichment.summary: Luke agrees that Tulliver would fare better remaining at the mill and expresses his own dislike of new places and changes.

chapter_title: An Item Added to the Family Register
text:
“But I doubt, Luke, they’ll be for getting rid o’ Ben, and
making you do with a lad; and I must help a bit wi’ the mill.
You’ll have a worse place.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Tulliver expresses practical concern about future layoffs, but dialogue is brief and expository without emotional or thematic weight.
enrichment.summary: Tulliver worries that Luke may be forced to work alongside a younger laborer and that his own situation will worsen.

chapter_title: An Item Added to the Family Register
text:
“Ne’er mind, sir,” said Luke, “I sha’n’t
plague mysen. I’n been wi’ you twenty year, an’ you
can’t get twenty year wi’ whistlin’ for ’em, no more
nor you can make the trees grow: you mun wait till God A’mighty sends
’em. I can’t abide new victual nor new faces,  I 
can’t,—you niver know but what they’ll gripe you.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Luke's loyalty is touching and reveals his character, but the dialogue is rambling and somewhat comic; it underscores themes of long-standing bonds and resistance to change.
enrichment.best_quote: I'n been wi' you twenty year, an' you can't get twenty year wi' whistlin' for 'em, no more nor you can make the trees grow
enrichment.summary: Luke expresses his loyalty to Tulliver, saying he has served him for twenty years and refuses to worry about changes or new circumstances.

chapter_title: An Item Added to the Family Register
text:
The walk was finished in silence after this, for Luke had disburthened himself
of thoughts to an extent that left his conversational resources quite barren,
and Mr Tulliver had relapsed from his recollections into a painful meditation
on the choice of hardships before him. Maggie noticed that he was unusually
absent that evening at tea; and afterward he sat leaning forward in his chair,
looking at the ground, moving his lips, and shaking his head from time to time.
Then he looked hard at Mrs Tulliver, who was knitting opposite him, then at
Maggie, who, as she bent over her sewing, was intensely conscious of some drama
going forward in her father’s mind. Suddenly he took up the poker and
broke the large coal fiercely.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Transitional paragraph marking a shift from nostalgic conversation to Tulliver's troubled meditation; alerts reader to Maggie's perception of drama and builds tension for the evening's events.
enrichment.summary: The walk ends in silence; Tulliver returns to painful meditation on his limited options, and Maggie notices his unusual abstraction at tea, sensing emotional turmoil.

chapter_title: An Item Added to the Family Register
text:
“Dear heart, Mr Tulliver, what can you be thinking of?” said his
wife, looking up in alarm; “it’s very wasteful, breaking the coal,
and we’ve got hardly any large coal left, and I don’t know where
the rest is to come from.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mrs. Tulliver's response is characteristically fussy and practical, revealing her domestic concerns, but the moment is brief and reflects her limited emotional range.
enrichment.summary: Mrs. Tulliver scolds her husband for wastefully breaking coal when supplies are running short.

chapter_title: An Item Added to the Family Register
text:
“I don’t think you’re quite so well to-night, are you,
father?” said Maggie; “you seem uneasy.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Maggie expresses concern for her father, but her brief dialogue is formulaic and does not advance plot or revelation substantially.
enrichment.summary: Maggie asks her father if he is feeling unwell, noticing his uneasiness.

chapter_title: An Item Added to the Family Register
text:
“Why, how is it Tom doesn’t come?” said Mr Tulliver,
impatiently.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Tulliver abruptly changes subject to ask about Tom; his impatience signals mounting agitation but dialogue itself is minimal.
enrichment.summary: Tulliver impatiently asks why Tom has not yet arrived home.

chapter_title: An Item Added to the Family Register
text:
“Dear heart! is it time? I must go and get his supper,” said Mrs
Tulliver, laying down her knitting, and leaving the room.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Purely functional, showing Mrs. Tulliver's domestic response with no emotional or thematic content.
enrichment.summary: Mrs. Tulliver realizes it is time to prepare Tom's supper and leaves the room.

chapter_title: An Item Added to the Family Register
text:
“It’s nigh upon half-past eight,” said Mr Tulliver.
“He’ll be here soon. Go, go and get the big Bible, and open it at
the beginning, where everything’s set down. And get the pen and
ink.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Tulliver's cryptic command to fetch the Bible and writing materials creates dramatic tension and foreshadows the solemn act to come; signals a turning point in his decision.
enrichment.summary: Tulliver tells Maggie to fetch the Bible and writing materials, indicating it is past half-past eight and Tom will arrive soon.

chapter_title: An Item Added to the Family Register
text:
Maggie obeyed, wondering; but her father gave no further orders, and only sat
listening for Tom’s footfall on the gravel, apparently irritated by the
wind, which had risen, and was roaring so as to drown all other sounds. There
was a strange light in his eyes that rather frightened Maggie;  she  began
to wish that Tom would come, too.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Maggie obeys and notices her father's strange, frightening demeanor and intensity; builds atmospheric tension and shows her intuitive anxiety about impending events.
enrichment.summary: Maggie brings the Bible and ink as instructed; her father listens anxiously for Tom while the wind roars outside, his strange intensity frightening Maggie.

chapter_title: An Item Added to the Family Register
text:
“There he is, then,” said Mr Tulliver, in an excited way, when the
knock came at last. Maggie went to open the door, but her mother came out of
the kitchen hurriedly, saying, “Stop a bit, Maggie; I’ll open
it.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Brief action showing Tulliver's excitement at Tom's arrival; functionally moves the scene forward but contains no substantial revelation or emotional depth.
enrichment.summary: Tom knocks at the door; Tulliver announces his arrival excitedly, but Mrs. Tulliver intercepts and insists on opening the door herself.

chapter_title: An Item Added to the Family Register
text:
Mrs Tulliver had begun to be a little frightened at her boy, but she was
jealous of every office others did for him.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Brief characterization of Mrs. Tulliver's protective jealousy over her son, adding color but not advancing the scene's central action substantially.
enrichment.summary: The narrator notes Mrs. Tulliver's protectiveness and jealousy regarding duties performed for her son Tom.

chapter_title: An Item Added to the Family Register
text:
“Your supper’s ready by the kitchen-fire, my boy,” she said,
as he took off his hat and coat. “You shall have it by yourself, just as
you like, and I won’t speak to you.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mrs. Tulliver's fussing over Tom is in character but offers little new information or emotional significance to the evening's drama.
enrichment.summary: Mrs. Tulliver offers Tom his supper by the kitchen fire and promises not to disturb him.

chapter_title: An Item Added to the Family Register
text:
“I think my father wants Tom, mother,” said Maggie; “he must
come into the parlour first.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Maggie's interruption directs Tom to his father, advancing the scene but with minimal emotional or dramatic weight.
enrichment.summary: Maggie tells her mother that their father needs Tom and he must come to the parlour first.

chapter_title: An Item Added to the Family Register
text:
Tom entered with his usual saddened evening face, but his eyes fell immediately
on the open Bible and the inkstand, and he glanced with a look of anxious
surprise at his father, who was saying,—

enrichment.interest_rationale: Tom notices the open Bible and inkstand and exchanges a glance of anxious surprise with his father, signaling his intuitive grasp that something momentous is about to occur.
enrichment.summary: Tom enters and immediately notices the open Bible and inkstand on the table, exchanging a look of anxious surprise with his father.

chapter_title: An Item Added to the Family Register
text: “Come, come, you’re late; I want you.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Purely functional dialogue; Tulliver merely tells Tom he is late, without substantial meaning.
enrichment.summary: Tulliver says Tom is late and that he wants him.

chapter_title: An Item Added to the Family Register
text: “Is there anything the matter, father?” said Tom.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Tom's query is natural and shows his concern, but the dialogue is brief and merely expresses anxiety about approaching events.
enrichment.summary: Tom asks if something is the matter with his father.

chapter_title: An Item Added to the Family Register
text: “You sit down, all of you,” said Mr Tulliver, peremptorily.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Purely directive; Tulliver orders everyone to sit down, functional staging with no emotional or thematic substance.
enrichment.summary: Tulliver peremptorily orders everyone to sit down.

chapter_title: An Item Added to the Family Register
text:
“And, Tom, sit down here; I’ve got something for you to write
i’ the Bible.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Tulliver directs Tom to sit and informs him of his intention to write something in the Bible, building tension but remaining brief and unexplained.
enrichment.summary: Tulliver tells Tom to sit and informs him that he has something to write in the Bible.

chapter_title: An Item Added to the Family Register
text:
They all three sat down, looking at him. He began to speak slowly, looking
first at his wife.

enrichment.interest_rationale: All three sit down as directed; the narrator notes their anxiety and that Tulliver speaks slowly and first addresses his wife, building dramatic anticipation.
enrichment.summary: All three family members sit and look at Tulliver; he speaks slowly, first addressing his wife.

chapter_title: An Item Added to the Family Register
text:
“I’ve made up my mind, Bessy, and I’ll be as good as my word
to you. There’ll be the same grave made for us to lie down in, and we
mustn’t be bearing one another ill-will. I’ll stop in the old
place, and I’ll serve under Wakem, and I’ll serve him like an
honest man; there’s no Tulliver but what’s honest, mind that,
Tom,”—here his voice rose,—“they’ll have it to
throw up against me as I paid a dividend, but it wasn’t my fault; it was
because there’s raskills in the world. They’ve been too many for
me, and I must give in. I’ll put my neck in harness,—for
you’ve a right to say as I’ve brought you into trouble,
Bessy,—and I’ll serve him as honest as if he was no raskill;
I’m an honest man, though I shall never hold my head up no more.
I’m a tree as is broke—a tree as is broke.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: The chapter's climactic moment: Tulliver announces his irrevocable decision to stay at the mill and work honestly under Wakem, fulfilling his pledge to Bessy while acknowledging his broken pride and powerlessness. This is the novel's turning point for his character arc and provides thematic resolution to the financial crisis.
enrichment.best_quote: I'm a tree as is broke—a tree as is broke.
enrichment.summary: Tulliver declares that he has made an irrevocable decision to remain at the mill and serve Wakem honestly, despite the humiliation, to honor his promise to Bessy; he acknowledges that he is powerless against the rascals and has lost his pride and independence.

chapter_title: An Item Added to the Family Register
text:
He paused and looked on the ground. Then suddenly raising his head, he said, in
a louder yet deeper tone:

enrichment.interest_rationale: Brief transitional pause as Tulliver prepares to speak again with renewed intensity; functionally marks a shift in his address but lacks substantial content.
enrichment.summary: Tulliver pauses and looks at the ground, then suddenly raises his head to speak in a louder, deeper tone.

chapter_title: An Item Added to the Family Register
text:
“But I won’t forgive him! I know what they say, he never meant me
any harm. That’s the way Old Harry props up the rascals. He’s been
at the bottom of everything; but he’s a fine gentleman,—I know, I
know. I shouldn’t ha’ gone to law, they say. But who made it so as
there was no arbitratin’, and no justice to be got? It signifies nothing
to him, I know that; he’s one o’ them fine gentlemen as get money
by doing business for poorer folks, and when he’s made beggars of
’em he’ll give ’em charity. I won’t forgive him! I wish
he might be punished with shame till his own son ’ud like to forget him.
I wish he may do summat as they’d make him work at the treadmill! But he
won’t,—he’s too big a raskill to let the law lay hold on him.
And you mind this, Tom,—you never forgive him neither, if you mean to be
my son. There’ll maybe come a time when you may make him feel;
it’ll never come to me; I’n got my head under the yoke. Now
write—write it i’ the Bible.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Tulliver's extraordinary tirade against Wakem reveals the deep bitterness beneath his outer resignation; a shathing critique of social injustice, hypocrisy, and the impunity of the wealthy, while demanding Tom perpetuate his vendetta. This passage is crucial to character, theme, and social commentary.
enrichment.best_quote: he's one o' them fine gentlemen as get money by doing business for poorer folks, and when he's made beggars of 'em he'll give 'em charity
enrichment.summary: Tulliver refuses to forgive Wakem despite claims that he never meant harm, exposing Wakem as a corrupt gentleman who profits from poor people's misfortune. He orders Tom to remember Wakem's cruelty and to make him suffer if the opportunity arises.

chapter_title: An Item Added to the Family Register
text:
“Oh, father, what?” said Maggie, sinking down by his knee, pale and
trembling. “It’s wicked to curse and bear malice.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Maggie's moral objection to her father's vindictiveness provides ethical counterpoint and reveals her tender conscience; foreshadows her later struggle between filial duty and moral principle.
enrichment.best_quote: It's wicked to curse and bear malice.
enrichment.summary: Maggie sinks down beside her father in tears and fear, begging him not to curse and bear malice, which she considers wicked.

chapter_title: An Item Added to the Family Register
text:
“It isn’t wicked, I tell you,” said her father, fiercely.
“It’s wicked as the raskills should prosper; it’s the
Devil’s doing. Do as I tell you, Tom. Write.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Tulliver's fierce dismissal of Maggie's morality reveals his hardened resolve and his belief that justice demands vengeance; establishes the conflict between Christian virtue and human righteous anger.
enrichment.summary: Tulliver angrily rejects Maggie's moral objection, insisting that it is wicked for rascals to prosper and that this is the Devil's doing, not his.

chapter_title: An Item Added to the Family Register
text: “What am I to write?” said Tom, with gloomy submission.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Tom's brief, reluctant acceptance of his father's authority shows his obedience and emotional resignation; minimal dialogue but significant in establishing his acquiescence to the burden being placed upon him.
enrichment.summary: Tom submits to his father's will and asks what he is to write.

chapter_title: An Item Added to the Family Register
text:
“Write as your father, Edward Tulliver, took service under John Wakem,
the man as had helped to ruin him, because I’d promised my wife to make
her what amends I could for her trouble, and because I wanted to die in
th’ old place where I was born and my father was born. Put that i’
the right words—you know how—and then write, as I don’t
forgive Wakem for all that; and for all I’ll serve him honest, I wish
evil may befall him. Write that.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Tulliver dictates the precise, solemn text to be written in the Bible, recording his name, his service to Wakem, his motivations (duty to Bessy and attachment to the old place), and his refusal to forgive—a binding document and historical record. Highly significant both narratively and thematically.
enrichment.best_quote: I don't forgive Wakem for all that; and for all I'll serve him honest, I wish evil may befall him.
enrichment.summary: Tulliver dictates to Tom a Bible entry recording that he has taken service under Wakem for love of his wife and attachment to the old mill, and that despite his honest service he will never forgive Wakem.

chapter_title: An Item Added to the Family Register
text:
There was a dead silence as Tom’s pen moved along the paper; Mrs
Tulliver looked scared, and Maggie trembled like a leaf.

enrichment.interest_rationale: The solemn silence as Tom writes conveys the gravity of the moment; Mrs. Tulliver's alarm and Maggie's trembling underscore the family's terror at this binding act.
enrichment.summary: Dead silence falls as Tom writes; Mrs. Tulliver looks frightened and Maggie trembles like a leaf at the solemnity of the act.

chapter_title: An Item Added to the Family Register
text:
“Now let me hear what you’ve wrote,” said Mr Tulliver. Tom
read aloud slowly.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Brief, functional scene where Tulliver requests to hear what has been written; no emotional or thematic substance, purely procedural.
enrichment.summary: Tulliver asks Tom to read aloud what he has written.

chapter_title: An Item Added to the Family Register
text:
“Now write—write as you’ll remember what Wakem’s done
to your father, and you’ll make him and his feel it, if ever the day
comes. And sign your name Thomas Tulliver.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Tulliver's final dictation demands that Tom memorialize his name and vow eternal vengeance against Wakem, binding the son to perpetuate the father's grievance into the future. This sealed covenant is the chapter's definitive act and establishes the vendetta that will haunt the family.
enrichment.best_quote: you'll make him and his feel it, if ever the day comes
enrichment.summary: Tulliver orders Tom to write that he will remember Wakem's cruelty and will make him and his family suffer when opportunity arises, then to sign his name as Thomas Tulliver.

chapter_title: An Item Added to the Family Register
text:
“Oh no, father, dear father!” said Maggie, almost choked with fear.
“You shouldn’t make Tom write that.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Maggie's final, anguished protest against compelling Tom to bind himself by oath mirrors her earlier moral objection; she senses the grave consequences and injustice of the demand.
enrichment.summary: Maggie cries out in anguish that her father should not make Tom write such a vow, fearing the binding nature of the promise.

chapter_title: An Item Added to the Family Register
text:
“Be quiet, Maggie!” said Tom. “I  shall  write
it.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Tom's calm, resolute acceptance of the burden contrasts sharply with Maggie's anguish and marks his acquiescence to become his father's agent of vengeance, establishing a central tension in his character arc.
enrichment.summary: Tom tells Maggie to be quiet and declares that he will write the vow, accepting his father's burden without hesitation.

chapter_title: Mr Riley Gives His Advice Concerning a School for Tom
text:
The gentleman in the ample white cravat and shirt-frill, taking his
brandy-and-water so pleasantly with his good friend Tulliver, is Mr Riley, a
gentleman with a waxen complexion and fat hands, rather highly educated for an
auctioneer and appraiser, but large-hearted enough to show a great deal of
 bonhomie  toward simple country acquaintances of hospitable habits. Mr
Riley spoke of such acquaintances kindly as “people of the old
school.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Introductory character description of Mr Riley establishing him as a hospitable auctioneer, routine exposition with no major plot or thematic significance.
enrichment.summary: Mr Riley, a waxen-complexioned auctioneer of considerable education, is presented as hospitable and genial toward country acquaintances like Tulliver.

chapter_title: Mr Riley Gives His Advice Concerning a School for Tom
text:
The conversation had come to a pause. Mr Tulliver, not without a particular
reason, had abstained from a seventh recital of the cool retort by which Riley
had shown himself too many for Dix, and how Wakem had had his comb cut for once
in his life, now the business of the dam had been settled by arbitration, and
how there never would have been any dispute at all about the height of water if
everybody was what they should be, and Old Harry hadn’t made the lawyers.
Mr Tulliver was, on the whole, a man of safe traditional opinions; but on one
or two points he had trusted to his unassisted intellect, and had arrived at
several questionable conclusions; amongst the rest, that rats, weevils, and
lawyers were created by Old Harry. Unhappily he had no one to tell him that
this was rampant Manichæism, else he might have seen his error. But to-day it
was clear that the good principle was triumphant: this affair of the
water-power had been a tangled business somehow, for all it seemed—look
at it one way—as plain as water’s water; but, big a puzzle as it
was, it hadn’t got the better of Riley. Mr Tulliver took his
brandy-and-water a little stronger than usual, and, for a man who might be
supposed to have a few hundreds lying idle at his banker’s, was rather
incautiously open in expressing his high estimate of his friend’s
business talents.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Reveals Tulliver's superstitious character (blaming lawyers and Old Harry) and his respect for Riley after a business dispute, with some comic social observation.
enrichment.best_quote: rats, weevils, and lawyers were created by Old Harry
enrichment.summary: Tulliver pauses in conversation after recounting Riley's victory over Dix and Wakem in a water-rights arbitration; Tulliver's folksy superstitions and estimation of Riley's talents are humorously detailed.

chapter_title: Mr Riley Gives His Advice Concerning a School for Tom
text:
But the dam was a subject of conversation that would keep; it could always be
taken up again at the same point, and exactly in the same condition; and there
was another subject, as you know, on which Mr Tulliver was in pressing want of
Mr Riley’s advice. This was his particular reason for remaining silent
for a short space after his last draught, and rubbing his knees in a meditative
manner. He was not a man to make an abrupt transition. This was a puzzling
world, as he often said, and if you drive your wagon in a hurry, you may light
on an awkward corner. Mr Riley, meanwhile, was not impatient. Why should he
be? Even Hotspur, one would think, must have been patient in his slippers on a
warm hearth, taking copious snuff, and sipping gratuitous brandy-and-water.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Transition paragraph signalling that Tulliver has a pressing matter to discuss with Riley; mostly connective prose with a light literary flourish comparing Riley to Hotspur.
enrichment.summary: Tulliver remains silent while considering how to raise his real purpose with Riley, an important matter about his son, while Riley contentedly takes snuff by the fire.

chapter_title: Mr Riley Gives His Advice Concerning a School for Tom
text:
“There’s a thing I’ve got i’ my head,” said Mr
Tulliver at last, in rather a lower tone than usual, as he turned his head and
looked steadfastly at his companion.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Brief dialogue tag marking the start of Tulliver's real concern; minimal interest as pure setup.
enrichment.summary: Tulliver begins to broach the subject he has been considering, speaking in a lower, more serious tone.

chapter_title: Mr Riley Gives His Advice Concerning a School for Tom
text:
“Ah!” said Mr Riley, in a tone of mild interest. He was a man with
heavy waxen eyelids and high-arched eyebrows, looking exactly the same under
all circumstances. This immovability of face, and the habit of taking a pinch
of snuff before he gave an answer, made him trebly oracular to Mr Tulliver.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Brief response and character detail about Riley's impassive features; minor characterization with comic potential but no significant development.
enrichment.summary: Riley responds with mild interest and his characteristic impassive expression, noted as giving him an oracular quality that impresses Tulliver.

chapter_title: Mr Riley Gives His Advice Concerning a School for Tom
text:
“It’s a very particular thing,” he went on; “it’s
about my boy Tom.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Simple dialogue announcing that the matter concerns Tom; purely functional setup with no inherent interest.
enrichment.summary: Tulliver states that his concern is about his boy Tom.

chapter_title: Mr Riley Gives His Advice Concerning a School for Tom
text:
At the sound of this name, Maggie, who was seated on a low stool close by the
fire, with a large book open on her lap, shook her heavy hair back and looked
up eagerly. There were few sounds that roused Maggie when she was dreaming over
her book, but Tom’s name served as well as the shrillest whistle; in an
instant she was on the watch, with gleaming eyes, like a Skye terrier
suspecting mischief, or at all events determined to fly at any one who
threatened it toward Tom.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Vivid introduction of Maggie's character and her fierce attachment to Tom, with memorable simile comparing her to a Skye terrier; establishes key character dynamic.
enrichment.best_quote: like a Skye terrier suspecting mischief, or at all events determined to fly at any one who threatened it toward Tom
enrichment.summary: Maggie, reading by the fire, instantly awakens at the mention of Tom's name, becoming alert and protective like a vigilant dog.

chapter_title: Mr Riley Gives His Advice Concerning a School for Tom
text:
“You see, I want to put him to a new school at Midsummer,” said Mr
Tulliver; “he’s comin’ away from the ’cademy at
Lady-day, an’ I shall let him run loose for a quarter; but after that I
want to send him to a downright good school, where they’ll make a
scholard of him.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Tulliver articulates his plan to send Tom to a better school; important for plot advancement and reveals his ambitions for his son's education.
enrichment.best_quote: he's comin' away from the 'cademy at Lady-day, an' I shall let him run loose for a quarter; but after that I want to send him to a downright good school, where they'll make a scholard of him
enrichment.summary: Tulliver explains that he intends to remove Tom from his current academy at Lady Day and after a quarter's break, place him at a superior school.

chapter_title: Mr Riley Gives His Advice Concerning a School for Tom
text:
“Well,” said Mr Riley, “there’s no greater advantage
you can give him than a good education. Not,” he added, with polite
significance,—“not that a man can’t be an excellent miller
and farmer, and a shrewd, sensible fellow into the bargain, without much help
from the schoolmaster.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Riley's diplomatic response acknowledging the value of education but noting it is not essential; largely perfunctory dialogue establishing Riley's conversational skill.
enrichment.summary: Riley agrees that education is valuable but diplomatically suggests that a man can succeed without formal schooling if he is sensible and practical.

chapter_title: Mr Riley Gives His Advice Concerning a School for Tom
text:
“I believe you,” said Mr Tulliver, winking, and turning his head
on one side; “but that’s where it is. I don’t  mean  Tom
to be a miller and farmer. I see no fun i’ that. Why, if I made him a
miller an’ farmer, he’d be expectin’ to take to the mill
an’ the land, an’ a-hinting at me as it was time for me to lay by
an’ think o’ my latter end. Nay, nay, I’ve seen enough
o’ that wi’ sons. I’ll never pull my coat off before I go to
bed. I shall give Tom an eddication an’ put him to a business, as he may
make a nest for himself, an’ not want to push me out o’ mine.
Pretty well if he gets it when I’m dead an’ gone. I
sha’n’t be put off wi’ spoon-meat afore I’ve lost my
teeth.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Tulliver reveals his fear that Tom will inherit the mill and displace him in old age, expressing strong anxiety about family succession and his own legacy; notable character psychology.
enrichment.best_quote: I'll never pull my coat off before I go to bed. I shall give Tom an eddication an' put him to a business, as he may make a nest for himself, an' not want to push me out o' mine
enrichment.summary: Tulliver insists he does not want Tom to become a miller and farmer, fearing his son would eventually want to take over the mill and pension off the old man.

chapter_title: Mr Riley Gives His Advice Concerning a School for Tom
text:
This was evidently a point on which Mr Tulliver felt strongly; and the impetus
which had given unusual rapidity and emphasis to his speech showed itself still
unexhausted for some minutes afterward in a defiant motion of the head from
side to side, and an occasional “Nay, nay,” like a subsiding growl.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Narrator notes Tulliver's emotional intensity on the subject, but offers only summary description rather than significant new information.
enrichment.summary: Tulliver's speech has stirred him to visible agitation, which subsides into defiant head shaking and muttered objections.

chapter_title: Mr Riley Gives His Advice Concerning a School for Tom
text:
These angry symptoms were keenly observed by Maggie, and cut her to the quick.
Tom, it appeared, was supposed capable of turning his father out of doors, and
of making the future in some way tragic by his wickedness. This was not to be
borne; and Maggie jumped up from her stool, forgetting all about her heavy
book, which fell with a bang within the fender, and going up between her
father’s knees, said, in a half-crying, half-indignant voice,—

enrichment.interest_rationale: Maggie's emotional response to her father's implied criticism of Tom is touching and reveals her protective love and fierce loyalty; strong character moment.
enrichment.best_quote: Father, Tom wouldn't be naughty to you ever; I know he wouldn't
enrichment.summary: Maggie jumps up defensively when she hears her father suggest Tom might betray him, rushing to Tom's defense with passionate indignation.

chapter_title: Mr Riley Gives His Advice Concerning a School for Tom
text:
“Father, Tom wouldn’t be naughty to you ever; I know he
wouldn’t.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Maggie's quoted defense of Tom; this is the continuation of her emotional outburst from P11.
enrichment.summary: Maggie insists that Tom would never be unkind or disloyal to their father.

chapter_title: Mr Riley Gives His Advice Concerning a School for Tom
text:
Mrs Tulliver was out of the room superintending a choice supper-dish, and Mr
Tulliver’s heart was touched; so Maggie was not scolded about the book.
Mr Riley quietly picked it up and looked at it, while the father laughed, with
a certain tenderness in his hard-lined face, and patted his little girl on the
back, and then held her hands and kept her between his knees.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Tulliver's tenderness toward Maggie and Riley's quiet observation reveal paternal affection and add warmth to the domestic scene, though narratively minor.
enrichment.best_quote: with a certain tenderness in his hard-lined face, and patted his little girl on the back
enrichment.summary: Mrs Tulliver is away attending to supper; Mr Tulliver is moved by Maggie's loyalty and shows her affection, while Riley picks up her fallen book.

chapter_title: Mr Riley Gives His Advice Concerning a School for Tom
text:
“What! they mustn’t say any harm o’ Tom, eh?” said Mr
Tulliver, looking at Maggie with a twinkling eye. Then, in a lower voice,
turning to Mr Riley, as though Maggie couldn’t hear, “She
understands what one’s talking about so as never was. And you should hear
her read,—straight off, as if she knowed it all beforehand. And allays at
her book! But it’s bad—it’s bad,” Mr Tulliver added
sadly, checking this blamable exultation. “A woman’s no business
wi’ being so clever; it’ll turn to trouble, I doubt. But bless
you!”—here the exultation was clearly recovering the
mastery,—“she’ll read the books and understand ’em
better nor half the folks as are growed up.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Tulliver's proud but worried assessment of Maggie's exceptional intellect, conflating her intelligence with danger to her future; important characterization and social critique on gender.
enrichment.best_quote: A woman's no business wi' being so clever; it'll turn to trouble, I doubt
enrichment.summary: Tulliver boasts of Maggie's precocious reading ability to Riley while simultaneously lamenting that her cleverness is a liability for a girl.

chapter_title: Mr Riley Gives His Advice Concerning a School for Tom
text:
Maggie’s cheeks began to flush with triumphant excitement. She thought
Mr Riley would have a respect for her now; it had been evident that he thought
nothing of her before.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Maggie's eager hope that Riley will now respect her intelligence is poignant and shows her hunger for recognition; brief but emotionally effective.
enrichment.summary: Maggie feels excited hope that Riley will now recognize her intelligence and worth, having previously dismissed her.

chapter_title: Mr Riley Gives His Advice Concerning a School for Tom
text:
Mr Riley was turning over the leaves of the book, and she could make nothing
of his face, with its high-arched eyebrows; but he presently looked at her, and
said,—

enrichment.interest_rationale: Brief description of Riley's examination of the book Maggie dropped; minimal plot significance.
enrichment.summary: Riley examines the book with an unreadable expression, his arched eyebrows revealing nothing.

chapter_title: Mr Riley Gives His Advice Concerning a School for Tom
text:
“Come, come and tell me something about this book; here are some
pictures,—I want to know what they mean.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Riley's invitation for Maggie to explain the book's pictures is a courteous gesture but purely functional dialogue leading to the next interaction.
enrichment.summary: Riley asks Maggie to explain the pictures in the book, showing polite interest.

chapter_title: Mr Riley Gives His Advice Concerning a School for Tom
text:
Maggie, with deepening colour, went without hesitation to Mr Riley’s
elbow and looked over the book, eagerly seizing one corner, and tossing back
her mane, while she said,—

enrichment.interest_rationale: Brief action showing Maggie approaching Riley eagerly; establishes the scene but lacks narrative weight.
enrichment.summary: Maggie eagerly joins Riley and looks at the book with him, her animation evident in her physical gesture.

chapter_title: Mr Riley Gives His Advice Concerning a School for Tom
text:
“Oh, I’ll tell you what that means. It’s a dreadful picture,
isn’t it? But I can’t help looking at it. That old woman in the
water’s a witch,—they’ve put her in to find out whether
she’s a witch or no; and if she swims she’s a witch, and if
she’s drowned—and killed, you know—she’s innocent, and
not a witch, but only a poor silly old woman. But what good would it do her
then, you know, when she was drowned? Only, I suppose, she’d go to
heaven, and God would make it up to her. And this dreadful blacksmith with his
arms akimbo, laughing,—oh, isn’t he ugly?—I’ll tell you
what he is. He’s the Devil  really ” (here Maggie’s
voice became louder and more emphatic), “and not a right blacksmith; for
the Devil takes the shape of wicked men, and walks about and sets people doing
wicked things, and he’s oftener in the shape of a bad man than any other,
because, you know, if people saw he was the Devil, and he roared at ’em,
they’d run away, and he couldn’t make ’em do what he
pleased.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Maggie's extraordinary and precocious theological discourse on witches, divine justice, and the Devil demonstrates her intellectual power and reveals her dark, passionate imagination; a showcase passage.
enrichment.best_quote: He's the Devil really, and not a right blacksmith; for the Devil takes the shape of wicked men, and walks about and sets people doing wicked things
enrichment.summary: Maggie launches into a detailed and passionate explanation of the witch-trial picture, elaborating on theodicy and the Devil's nature with precocious theological insight.

chapter_title: Mr Riley Gives His Advice Concerning a School for Tom
text:
Mr Tulliver had listened to this exposition of Maggie’s with petrifying
wonder.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Narrator's one-sentence summary of Mr Tulliver's stunned reaction; minimal content, purely transitional.
enrichment.summary: Mr Tulliver is astonished by Maggie's discourse.

chapter_title: Mr Riley Gives His Advice Concerning a School for Tom
text:
“Why, what book is it the wench has got hold on?” he burst out at
last.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Tulliver's exclamation questioning the book's origin; minor dialogue tag, functionally important but not inherently interesting.
enrichment.summary: Mr Tulliver interrupts with shock, asking what book Maggie has been reading.

chapter_title: Mr Riley Gives His Advice Concerning a School for Tom
text:
“‘The History of the Devil,’ by Daniel Defoe,—not quite
the right book for a little girl,” said Mr Riley. “How came it
among your books, Mr Tulliver?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Riley identifies the book as 'The History of the Devil' by Defoe and judges it inappropriate for a girl; introduces the book mystery while establishing Riley's conventional propriety.
enrichment.best_quote: 'The History of the Devil,' by Daniel Defoe,—not quite the right book for a little girl
enrichment.summary: Riley identifies the book and notes disapprovingly that it is inappropriate reading for a child.

chapter_title: Mr Riley Gives His Advice Concerning a School for Tom
text: Maggie looked hurt and discouraged, while her father said,—

enrichment.interest_rationale: Brief notation of Maggie's hurt at the implicit criticism; emotionally understandable but narratively minimal.
enrichment.summary: Maggie looks hurt and discouraged by Riley's reproach.

chapter_title: Mr Riley Gives His Advice Concerning a School for Tom
text:
“Why, it’s one o’ the books I bought at Partridge’s
sale. They was all bound alike,—it’s a good binding, you
see,—and I thought they’d be all good books. There’s Jeremy
Taylor’s ‘Holy Living and Dying’ among ’em. I read in
it often of a Sunday” (Mr Tulliver felt somehow a familiarity with that
great writer, because his name was Jeremy); “and there’s a lot more
of ’em,—sermons mostly, I think,—but they’ve all got
the same covers, and I thought they were all o’ one sample, as you may
say. But it seems one mustn’t judge by th’ outside. This is a
puzzlin’ world.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Tulliver's explanation that he bought the books as a set without examining them individually reveals his innocent carelessness and offers social satire on provincial book purchasing.
enrichment.best_quote: I thought they were all o' one sample, as you may say. But it seems one mustn't judge by th' outside. This is a puzzlin' world
enrichment.summary: Mr Tulliver explains that he purchased the books at an auction as a job lot, assuming uniform quality based on matching bindings.

chapter_title: Mr Riley Gives His Advice Concerning a School for Tom
text:
“Well,” said Mr Riley, in an admonitory, patronizing tone as he
patted Maggie on the head, “I advise you to put by the ‘History of
the Devil,’ and read some prettier book. Have you no prettier
books?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Riley's patronizing advice to Maggie to read prettier books; conventional moral instruction with no real substance.
enrichment.summary: Riley advises Maggie to put aside the History of the Devil and read more suitable books.

chapter_title: Mr Riley Gives His Advice Concerning a School for Tom
text:
“Oh, yes,” said Maggie, reviving a little in the desire to
vindicate the variety of her reading. “I know the reading in this book
isn’t pretty; but I like the pictures, and I make stories to the pictures
out of my own head, you know. But I’ve got ‘Æsop’s
Fables,’ and a book about Kangaroos and things, and the
‘Pilgrim’s Progress....’”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Maggie defends her reading and lists her other books, including Pilgrim's Progress; shows her knowledge and eagerness to be thought well of.
enrichment.best_quote: I like the pictures, and I make stories to the pictures out of my own head, you know
enrichment.summary: Maggie explains that she creates her own narratives from the pictures and lists her other reading, including Aesop's Fables and Pilgrim's Progress.

chapter_title: Mr Riley Gives His Advice Concerning a School for Tom
text:
“Ah, a beautiful book,” said Mr Riley; “you can’t read
a better.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Riley's brief approving comment on Pilgrim's Progress; minimal content, purely functional dialogue tag.
enrichment.summary: Riley praises Pilgrim's Progress as an excellent book.

chapter_title: Mr Riley Gives His Advice Concerning a School for Tom
text:
“Well, but there’s a great deal about the Devil in that,”
said Maggie, triumphantly, “and I’ll show you the picture of him in
his true shape, as he fought with Christian.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Maggie triumphantly notes that Pilgrim's Progress also contains Devil content, showing her intelligence and ability to catch Riley in hypocrisy; quick-witted character moment.
enrichment.best_quote: Well, but there's a great deal about the Devil in that, and I'll show you the picture of him in his true shape, as he fought with Christian
enrichment.summary: Maggie triumphantly points out that Pilgrim's Progress also contains Devil content, offering to show Riley the picture of the Devil fighting Christian.

chapter_title: Mr Riley Gives His Advice Concerning a School for Tom
text:
Maggie ran in an instant to the corner of the room, jumped on a chair, and
reached down from the small bookcase a shabby old copy of Bunyan, which opened
at once, without the least trouble of search, at the picture she wanted.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Description of Maggie's action retrieving the book; minor movement, adds liveliness but no significant narrative content.
enrichment.summary: Maggie quickly retrieves her worn copy of Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress from the bookcase, which opens immediately to the desired illustration.

chapter_title: Mr Riley Gives His Advice Concerning a School for Tom
text:
“Here he is,” she said, running back to Mr Riley, “and Tom
coloured him for me with his paints when he was at home last
holidays,—the body all black, you know, and the eyes red, like fire,
because he’s all fire inside, and it shines out at his eyes.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Maggie shows the Devil illustration to Riley, noting that Tom colored it with his paints; demonstrates sibling affection and artistic creativity.
enrichment.best_quote: Tom coloured him for me with his paints when he was at home last holidays,—the body all black, you know, and the eyes red, like fire
enrichment.summary: Maggie presents the picture to Riley, explaining that Tom colored the Devil figure in his typical holidays with black body and red eyes.

chapter_title: Mr Riley Gives His Advice Concerning a School for Tom
text:
“Go, go!” said Mr Tulliver, peremptorily, beginning to feel rather
uncomfortable at these free remarks on the personal appearance of a being
powerful enough to create lawyers; “shut up the book, and let’s
hear no more o’ such talk. It is as I thought—the child ’ull
learn more mischief nor good wi’ the books. Go, go and see after your
mother.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mr Tulliver's discomfort with Maggie's theological talk and his abrupt dismissal reveal his anxiety about excessive discussion of dangerous spiritual subjects; shows parental concern.
enrichment.best_quote: shut up the book, and let's hear no more o' such talk. It is as I thought—the child 'ull learn more mischief nor good wi' the books
enrichment.summary: Tulliver feels uncomfortable with Maggie's frank theological discourse and commands her to close the book and cease her remarks about the Devil.

chapter_title: Mr Riley Gives His Advice Concerning a School for Tom
text:
Maggie shut up the book at once, with a sense of disgrace, but not being
inclined to see after her mother, she compromised the matter by going into a
dark corner behind her father’s chair, and nursing her doll, toward which
she had an occasional fit of fondness in Tom’s absence, neglecting its
toilet, but lavishing so many warm kisses on it that the waxen cheeks had a
wasted, unhealthy appearance.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Maggie's response to her father's rebuke—obedience mixed with emotional withdrawal—is touching; her self-consolation with her doll shows childish coping.
enrichment.summary: Maggie obeys her father's command but retreats into a corner to nurse her doll instead of checking on her mother, processing her shame through self-soothing play.

chapter_title: Mr Riley Gives His Advice Concerning a School for Tom
text:
“Did you ever hear the like on’t?” said Mr Tulliver, as
Maggie retired. “It’s a pity but what she’d been the
lad,—she’d ha’ been a match for the lawyers,  she 
would. It’s the wonderful’st thing”—here he lowered his
voice—“as I picked the mother because she wasn’t o’er
’cute—bein’ a good-looking woman too, an’ come of a
rare family for managing; but I picked her from her sisters o’ purpose,
’cause she was a bit weak like; for I wasn’t agoin’ to be
told the rights o’ things by my own fireside. But you see when a
man’s got brains himself, there’s no knowing where they’ll
run to; an’ a pleasant sort o’ soft woman may go on breeding you
stupid lads and ’cute wenches, till it’s like as if the world was
turned topsy-turvy. It’s an uncommon puzzlin’ thing.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Tulliver's rueful reflection on Maggie's precocious intellect, expressed as astonishment at his own role in producing such an inconvenient daughter, is both comic and reveals his anxious sexism.
enrichment.best_quote: It's a pity but what she'd been the lad,—she'd ha' been a match for the lawyers, she would
enrichment.summary: Tulliver laments to Riley that Maggie's cleverness would be invaluable in a boy but is problematic in a girl, revealing that he deliberately married a simple woman to avoid being dominated by an intelligent wife.

chapter_title: Mr Riley Gives His Advice Concerning a School for Tom
text:
Mr Riley’s gravity gave way, and he shook a little under the application
of his pinch of snuff before he said,—

enrichment.interest_rationale: Brief notation of Riley's suppressed amusement; transitional moment with minimal content.
enrichment.summary: Riley struggles to maintain his grave composure as he takes snuff, evidently amused by Tulliver's candid admission.

chapter_title: Mr Riley Gives His Advice Concerning a School for Tom
text:
“But your lad’s not stupid, is he? I saw him, when I was here last,
busy making fishing-tackle; he seemed quite up to it.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Riley's brief reminder that Tom is not stupid, based on observing his fishing-tackle; minor reassurance, functionally important but not inherently interesting.
enrichment.summary: Riley observes that Tom showed sense and capability when making fishing-tackle on his previous visit.

chapter_title: Mr Riley Gives His Advice Concerning a School for Tom
text:
“Well, he isn’t not to say stupid,—he’s got a notion
o’ things out o’ door, an’ a sort o’ common sense, as
he’d lay hold o’ things by the right handle. But he’s slow
with his tongue, you see, and he reads but poorly, and can’t abide the
books, and spells all wrong, they tell me, an’ as shy as can be wi’
strangers, an’ you never hear him say ’cute things like the little
wench. Now, what I want is to send him to a school where they’ll make him
a bit nimble with his tongue and his pen, and make a smart chap of him. I want
my son to be even wi’ these fellows as have got the start o’ me
with having better schooling. Not but what, if the world had been left as God
made it, I could ha’ seen my way, and held my own wi’ the best of
’em; but things have got so twisted round and wrapped up i’
unreasonable words, as aren’t a bit like ’em, as I’m clean at
fault, often an’ often. Everything winds about so—the more
straightforrad you are, the more you’re puzzled.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Tulliver's detailed explanation of Tom's limitations and his desire for education that will sharpen his commercial skills reveals both his assessment of his son and his anxieties about incompetence in a complex world.
enrichment.best_quote: Everything winds about so—the more straightforrad you are, the more you're puzzled
enrichment.summary: Tulliver characterizes Tom as practical but slow with language and weak in reading, and expresses his desire for a school that will make Tom sharp and competent in business and communication.

chapter_title: Mr Riley Gives His Advice Concerning a School for Tom
text:
Mr Tulliver took a draught, swallowed it slowly, and shook his head in a
melancholy manner, conscious of exemplifying the truth that a perfectly sane
intellect is hardly at home in this insane world.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Narrator's brief summary of Tulliver's melancholic consciousness; atmospheric but minimal substantive content.
enrichment.summary: Tulliver pauses with evident sadness, embodying the truth that a sane intellect struggles in an insane world.

chapter_title: Mr Riley Gives His Advice Concerning a School for Tom
text:
“You’re quite in the right of it, Tulliver,” observed Mr
Riley. “Better spend an extra hundred or two on your son’s
education, than leave it him in your will. I know I should have tried to do so
by a son of mine, if I’d had one, though, God knows, I haven’t your
ready money to play with, Tulliver; and I have a houseful of daughters into the
bargain.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Riley's agreement and gentle boast about his own prudence; conversational filler with little substance.
enrichment.summary: Riley affirms Tulliver's wisdom about education and self-deprecatingly notes his own lack of ready capital and abundance of daughters.

chapter_title: Mr Riley Gives His Advice Concerning a School for Tom
text:
“I dare say, now, you know of a school as ’ud be just the thing for
Tom,” said Mr Tulliver, not diverted from his purpose by any sympathy
with Mr Riley’s deficiency of ready cash.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Tulliver's direct request for Riley's advice on schools; functionally important but purely expository dialogue.
enrichment.summary: Tulliver presses Riley for a recommendation of a suitable school for Tom.

chapter_title: Mr Riley Gives His Advice Concerning a School for Tom
text:
Mr Riley took a pinch of snuff, and kept Mr Tulliver in suspense by a silence
that seemed deliberative, before he said,—
