chapter_title: Mr Tulliver Shows His Weaker Side
text:
Mr Tulliver, when under the influence of a strong feeling, had a promptitude
in action that may seem inconsistent with that painful sense of the
complicated, puzzling nature of human affairs under which his more
dispassionate deliberations were conducted; but it is really not improbable
that there was a direct relation between these apparently contradictory
phenomena, since I have observed that for getting a strong impression that a
skein is tangled there is nothing like snatching hastily at a single thread. It
was owing to this promptitude that Mr Tulliver was on horseback soon after
dinner the next day (he was not dyspeptic) on his way to Basset to see his
sister Moss and her husband. For having made up his mind irrevocably that he
would pay Mrs Glegg her loan of five hundred pounds, it naturally occurred to
him that he had a promissory note for three hundred pounds lent to his
brother-in-law Moss; and if the said brother-in-law could manage to pay in the
money within a given time, it would go far to lessen the fallacious air of
inconvenience which Mr Tulliver’s spirited step might have worn in the
eyes of weak people who require to know precisely  how  a thing is to be
done before they are strongly confident that it will be easy.

enrichment.interest_rationale: An exceptionally revealing passage combining deep character psychology, narratorial commentary on the paradox of Mr Tulliver's impulsive action, and the crucial plot device of the promissory note to Moss.
enrichment.best_quote: it is really not improbable that there was a direct relation between these apparently contradictory phenomena, since I have observed that for getting a strong impression that a skein is tangled there is nothing like snatching hastily at a single thread.
enrichment.summary: The narrator explains Mr Tulliver's characteristic pattern: his impulsive decisiveness when emotionally aroused, contrasting with his usual recognition of life's complexity; he decides to call in Moss's three-hundred-pound debt to offset his own obligation to Mrs Glegg.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver Shows His Weaker Side
text:
For Mr Tulliver was in a position neither new nor striking, but, like other
everyday things, sure to have a cumulative effect that will be felt in the
long run: he was held to be a much more substantial man than he really was. And
as we are all apt to believe what the world believes about us, it was his habit
to think of failure and ruin with the same sort of remote pity with which a
spare, long-necked man hears that his plethoric short-necked neighbour is
stricken with apoplexy. He had been always used to hear pleasant jokes about
his advantages as a man who worked his own mill, and owned a pretty bit of
land; and these jokes naturally kept up his sense that he was a man of
considerable substance. They gave a pleasant flavour to his glass on a
market-day, and if it had not been for the recurrence of half-yearly payments,
Mr Tulliver would really have forgotten that there was a mortgage of two
thousand pounds on his very desirable freehold. That was not altogether his own
fault, since one of the thousand pounds was his sister’s fortune, which
he had to pay on her marriage; and a man who has neighbours that  will  go
to law with him is not likely to pay off his mortgages, especially if he enjoys
the good opinion of acquaintances who want to borrow a hundred pounds on
security too lofty to be represented by parchment. Our friend Mr Tulliver had
a good-natured fibre in him, and did not like to give harsh refusals even to
his sister, who had not only come in to the world in that superfluous way
characteristic of sisters, creating a necessity for mortgages, but had quite
thrown herself away in marriage, and had crowned her mistakes by having an
eighth baby. On this point Mr Tulliver was conscious of being a little weak;
but he apologised to himself by saying that poor Gritty had been a good-looking
wench before she married Moss; he would sometimes say this even with a slight
tremulousness in his voice. But this morning he was in a mood more becoming a
man of business, and in the course of his ride along the Basset lanes, with
their deep ruts,—lying so far away from a market-town that the labour of
drawing produce and manure was enough to take away the best part of the profits
on such poor land as that parish was made of,—he got up a due amount of
irritation against Moss as a man without capital, who, if murrain and blight
were abroad, was sure to have his share of them, and who, the more you tried to
help him out of the mud, would sink the further in. It would do him good rather
than harm, now, if he were obliged to raise this three hundred pounds; it would
make him look about him better, and not act so foolishly about his wool this
year as he did the last; in fact, Mr Tulliver had been too easy with his
brother-in-law, and because he had let the interest run on for two years, Moss
was likely enough to think that he should never be troubled about the
principal. But Mr Tulliver was determined not to encourage such shuffling
people any longer; and a ride along the Basset lanes was not likely to enervate
a man’s resolution by softening his temper. The deep-trodden hoof-marks,
made in the muddiest days of winter, gave him a shake now and then which
suggested a rash but stimulating snarl at the father of lawyers, who, whether
by means of his hoof or otherwise, had doubtless something to do with this
state of the roads; and the abundance of foul land and neglected fences that
met his eye, though they made no part of his brother Moss’s farm,
strongly contributed to his dissatisfaction with that unlucky agriculturist. If
this wasn’t Moss’s fallow, it might have been; Basset was all
alike; it was a beggarly parish, in Mr Tulliver’s opinion, and his
opinion was certainly not groundless. Basset had a poor soil, poor roads, a
poor non-resident landlord, a poor non-resident vicar, and rather less than
half a curate, also poor. If any one strongly impressed with the power of the
human mind to triumph over circumstances will contend that the parishioners of
Basset might nevertheless have been a very superior class of people, I have
nothing to urge against that abstract proposition; I only know that, in point
of fact, the Basset mind was in strict keeping with its circumstances. The
muddy lanes, green or clayey, that seemed to the unaccustomed eye to lead
nowhere but into each other, did really lead, with patience, to a distant
high-road; but there were many feet in Basset which they led more frequently to
a centre of dissipation, spoken of formerly as the “Markis o’
Granby,” but among intimates as “Dickison’s.” A large
low room with a sanded floor; a cold scent of tobacco, modified by undetected
beer-dregs; Mr Dickison leaning against the door-post with a melancholy
pimpled face, looking as irrelevant to the daylight as a last night’s
guttered candle,—all this may not seem a very seductive form of
temptation; but the majority of men in Basset found it fatally alluring when
encountered on their road toward four o’clock on a wintry afternoon; and
if any wife in Basset wished to indicate that her husband was not a
pleasure-seeking man, she could hardly do it more emphatically than by saying
that he didn’t spend a shilling at Dickison’s from one Whitsuntide
to another. Mrs Moss had said so of  her  husband more than once, when
her brother was in a mood to find fault with him, as he certainly was to-day.
And nothing could be less pacifying to Mr Tulliver than the behaviour of the
farmyard gate, which he no sooner attempted to push open with his riding-stick
than it acted as gates without the upper hinge are known to do, to the peril of
shins, whether equine or human. He was about to get down and lead his horse
through the damp dirt of the hollow farmyard, shadowed drearily by the large
half-timbered buildings, up to the long line of tumble-down dwelling-houses
standing on a raised causeway; but the timely appearance of a cowboy saved him
that frustration of a plan he had determined on,—namely, not to get down
from his horse during this visit. If a man means to be hard, let him keep in
his saddle and speak from that height, above the level of pleading eyes, and
with the command of a distant horizon. Mrs Moss heard the sound of the
horse’s feet, and, when her brother rode up, was already outside the
kitchen door, with a half-weary smile on her face, and a black-eyed baby in her
arms. Mrs Moss’s face bore a faded resemblance to her brother’s;
baby’s little fat hand, pressed against her cheek, seemed to show more
strikingly that the cheek was faded.

enrichment.interest_rationale: A masterful social analysis revealing Mr Tulliver's financial delusion and moral weakness through extended ironic commentary on his self-deception, his sister Gritty's plight, and Basset parish itself—central to understanding his character and the novel's critique of provincial life.
enrichment.best_quote: He had been always used to hear pleasant jokes about his advantages as a man who worked his own mill, and owned a pretty bit of land; and these jokes naturally kept up his sense that he was a man of considerable substance.
enrichment.summary: The narrator exposes Mr Tulliver's false sense of security despite carrying a two-thousand-pound mortgage, his unconscious blindness to his sister's suffering, and his weakness in lending to Moss; the passage then provides a scathing sociological portrait of Basset parish, its poor soil, poverty, and the temptations of Dickison's public house.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver Shows His Weaker Side
text:
“Brother, I’m glad to see you,” she said, in an affectionate
tone. “I didn’t look for you to-day. How do you do?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: A simple greeting establishing Mrs Moss's affectionate but anxious demeanor; routine dialogue.
enrichment.summary: Mrs Moss greets her brother warmly and asks how he is doing, unaware of his unsettled mood.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver Shows His Weaker Side
text:
“Oh, pretty well, Mrs Moss, pretty well,” answered the brother,
with cool deliberation, as if it were rather too forward of her to ask that
question. She knew at once that her brother was not in a good humour; he never
called her Mrs Moss except when he was angry, and when they were in company.
But she thought it was in the order of nature that people who were poorly off
should be snubbed. Mrs Moss did not take her stand on the equality of the
human race; she was a patient, prolific, loving-hearted woman.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Reveals Mrs Moss's perceptiveness regarding her brother's anger and her resigned acceptance of social inequality; adds psychological depth to her character.
enrichment.best_quote: She knew at once that her brother was not in a good humour; he never called her Mrs Moss except when he was angry, and when they were in company.
enrichment.summary: Mr Tulliver replies coolly to Mrs Moss's greeting, and she quickly perceives his displeasure from his formal address; she philosophically accepts the natural order of the poor being snubbed.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver Shows His Weaker Side
text:
“Your husband isn’t in the house, I suppose?” added Mr
Tulliver after a grave pause, during which four children had run out, like
chickens whose mother has been suddenly in eclipse behind the hen-coop.

enrichment.interest_rationale: A brief expository question moving the scene forward; routine dialogue.
enrichment.summary: Mr Tulliver asks if Mr Moss is in the house, implying he wishes to speak with him rather than his sister.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver Shows His Weaker Side
text:
“No,” said Mrs Moss, “but he’s only in the
potato-field yonders. Georgy, run to the Far Close in a minute, and tell father
your uncle’s come. You’ll get down, brother, won’t you, and
take something?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Routine domestic exchanges with no distinctive content or character revelation.
enrichment.summary: Mrs Moss reports Mr Moss is in the potato field and offers hospitality, which Mr Tulliver declines.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver Shows His Weaker Side
text:
“No, no; I can’t get down. I must be going home again
directly,” said Mr Tulliver, looking at the distance.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Minimal dialogue; a simple refusal.
enrichment.summary: Mr Tulliver refuses to dismount or take refreshment, saying he must depart soon.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver Shows His Weaker Side
text:
“And how’s Mrs Tulliver and the children?” said Mrs Moss,
humbly, not daring to press her invitation.

enrichment.interest_rationale: A courteous but formulaic social enquiry.
enrichment.summary: Mrs Moss humbly enquires after Mrs Tulliver and the children.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver Shows His Weaker Side
text:
“Oh, pretty well. Tom’s going to a new school at Midsummer,—a
deal of expense to me. It’s bad work for me, lying out o’ my
money.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Introduces Tom's schooling expense as a financial burden, relevant to the plot but delivered matter-of-factly.
enrichment.best_quote: It's bad work for me, lying out o' my money.
enrichment.summary: Mr Tulliver mentions that Tom will attend a new school at Midsummer, which represents considerable expense and ties up his capital.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver Shows His Weaker Side
text:
“I wish you’d be so good as let the children come and see their
cousins some day. My little uns want to see their cousin Maggie so as never
was. And me her godmother, and so fond of her; there’s nobody ’ud
make a bigger fuss with her, according to what they’ve got. And I know
she likes to come, for she’s a loving child, and how quick and clever she
is, to be sure!”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mrs Moss's praise of Maggie reveals her affection, her role as godmother, and her own maternal tenderness; it becomes the emotional turning point of the scene.
enrichment.best_quote: My little uns want to see their cousin Maggie so as never was.
enrichment.summary: Mrs Moss appeals for the children to visit, expressing her affection for Maggie and admiration of her intelligence and loving nature.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver Shows His Weaker Side
text:
If Mrs Moss had been one of the most astute women in the world, instead of
being one of the simplest, she could have thought of nothing more likely to
propitiate her brother than this praise of Maggie. He seldom found any one
volunteering praise of “the little wench”; it was usually left
entirely to himself to insist on her merits. But Maggie always appeared in the
most amiable light at her aunt Moss’s; it was her Alsatia, where she was
out of the reach of law,—if she upset anything, dirtied her shoes, or
tore her frock, these things were matters of course at her aunt Moss’s.
In spite of himself, Mr Tulliver’s eyes got milder, and he did not look
away from his sister as he said,—

enrichment.interest_rationale: The narrator explains that Mrs Moss's innocent praise of Maggie uniquely appeals to Mr Tulliver's vulnerability, introducing the metaphor of Maggie's aunt's house as 'Alsatia' and signaling the emotional shift that will reverse his harshness.
enrichment.best_quote: it was her Alsatia, where she was out of the reach of law,—if she upset anything, dirtied her shoes, or tore her frock, these things were matters of course at her aunt Moss's.
enrichment.summary: The narrator reveals that Maggie holds a special place in Mr Tulliver's heart and that aunt Moss's house is a sanctuary for Maggie; the praise of her softens his demeanor toward his sister.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver Shows His Weaker Side
text:
“Ay; she’s fonder o’ you than o’ the other aunts, I
think. She takes after our family: not a bit of her mother’s in
her.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mr Tulliver's affectionate remark about Maggie being more like his family than her mother's shows parental pride, though brief and somewhat dismissive of his wife.
enrichment.best_quote: She takes after our family: not a bit of her mother's in her.
enrichment.summary: Mr Tulliver affirms that Maggie resembles his family more than her mother's, and that she prefers her aunt Moss's company.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver Shows His Weaker Side
text:
“Moss says she’s just like what I used to be,” said Mrs
Moss, “though I was never so quick and fond o’ the books. But I
think my Lizzy’s like her;  she’s  sharp. Come here, Lizzy, my
dear, and let your uncle see you; he hardly knows you, you grow so fast.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mrs Moss's comment that Lizzy resembles her younger self provides a moment of female kinship and connection, though modest in scope.
enrichment.best_quote: Moss says she's just like what I used to be.
enrichment.summary: Mrs Moss remarks that her daughter Lizzy resembles herself in her youth, though not as quick or bookish as Maggie, and calls Lizzy forward to greet her uncle.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver Shows His Weaker Side
text:
Lizzy, a black-eyed child of seven, looked very shy when her mother drew her
forward, for the small Mosses were much in awe of their uncle from Dorlcote
Mill. She was inferior enough to Maggie in fire and strength of expression to
make the resemblance between the two entirely flattering to Mr
Tulliver’s fatherly love.

enrichment.interest_rationale: A brief observation on Lizzy's shyness and her difference from Maggie, delivered to flatter Mr Tulliver's paternal pride.
enrichment.summary: The narrator notes that Lizzy is shy and inferior in spirit and expression to Maggie, making the family resemblance flattering to Mr Tulliver's pride in his daughter.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver Shows His Weaker Side
text:
“Ay, they’re a bit alike,” he said, looking kindly at the
little figure in the soiled pinafore. “They both take after our mother.
You’ve got enough o’ gells, Gritty,” he added, in a tone half
compassionate, half reproachful.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mr Tulliver acknowledges the family resemblance and makes a mild reproach about Mrs Moss having too many daughters, showing his growing kindliness toward her.
enrichment.best_quote: You've got enough o' gells, Gritty.
enrichment.summary: Mr Tulliver looks kindly at Lizzy and remarks that the girls resemble their mother, while adding a half-compassionate, half-reproachful comment about Mrs Moss having so many daughters.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver Shows His Weaker Side
text:
“Four of ’em, bless ’em!” said Mrs Moss, with a sigh,
stroking Lizzy’s hair on each side of her forehead; “as many as
there’s boys. They’ve got a brother apiece.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mrs Moss's affectionate acceptance of her large family is character-establishing but formulaic.
enrichment.best_quote: Four of 'em, bless 'em!
enrichment.summary: Mrs Moss responds with affectionate resignation, noting she has four daughters balanced by brothers for each, as she strokes Lizzy's hair.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver Shows His Weaker Side
text:
“Ah, but they must turn out and fend for themselves,” said Mr
Tulliver, feeling that his severity was relaxing and trying to brace it by
throwing out a wholesome hint “They mustn’t look to hanging on
their brothers.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mr Tulliver offers a conventional moral about daughters needing to be independent, but his severity is noticeably relaxing.
enrichment.best_quote: They mustn't look to hanging on their brothers.
enrichment.summary: Mr Tulliver advises that the daughters must become self-supporting rather than dependent on their brothers, while sensing his own severity is softening.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver Shows His Weaker Side
text:
“No; but I hope their brothers ’ull love the poor things, and
remember they came o’ one father and mother; the lads ’ull never be
the poorer for that,” said Mrs Moss, flashing out with hurried timidity,
like a half-smothered fire.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mrs Moss's passionate but timid response about brotherly love reveals her moral priorities and emotional intensity beneath her outward patience.
enrichment.best_quote: I hope their brothers 'ull love the poor things, and remember they came o' one father and mother; the lads 'ull never be the poorer for that.
enrichment.summary: Mrs Moss passionately insists that brothers should love their sisters out of family feeling and shared lineage, refusing the purely economic view.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver Shows His Weaker Side
text:
Mr Tulliver gave his horse a little stroke on the flank, then checked it, and
said angrily, “Stand still with you!” much to the astonishment of
that innocent animal.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mr Tulliver's irritated gesture at his horse reveals his emotional response to Mrs Moss's moral appeal but is otherwise a brief action beat.
enrichment.best_quote: Stand still with you!
enrichment.summary: Mr Tulliver strikes his horse irritably, puzzling the animal, revealing his agitation at his sister's words.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver Shows His Weaker Side
text:
“And the more there is of ’em, the more they must love one
another,” Mrs Moss went on, looking at her children with a didactic
purpose. But she turned toward her brother again to say, “Not but what I
hope your boy ’ull allays be good to his sister, though there’s but
two of ’em, like you and me, brother.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mrs Moss continues her moral instruction, drawing a parallel between her own large family and the need for sibling love, then pivots to hope that Tom will be good to Maggie.
enrichment.best_quote: I hope your boy 'ull allays be good to his sister, though there's but two of 'em, like you and me, brother.
enrichment.summary: Mrs Moss expands her teaching about sibling love to apply specifically to Tom and Maggie, noting the parallel to her relationship with Mr Tulliver.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver Shows His Weaker Side
text:
The arrow went straight to Mr Tulliver’s heart. He had not a rapid
imagination, but the thought of Maggie was very near to him, and he was not
long in seeing his relation to his own sister side by side with Tom’s
relation to Maggie. Would the little wench ever be poorly off, and Tom rather
hard upon her?

enrichment.interest_rationale: The emotional and thematic crux of the scene: Mr Tulliver's meditation on Maggie's future vulnerability and his sudden identification with his sister through the lens of Tom's relationship to Maggie—a profound moment of moral insight.
enrichment.best_quote: Would the little wench ever be poorly off, and Tom rather hard upon her?
enrichment.summary: The arrow of Mrs Moss's comment strikes Mr Tulliver's heart as he visualizes Maggie's future dependence on Tom and sees his own relationship to Gritty mirrored in Tom's likely future relationship to his sister.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver Shows His Weaker Side

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mr Tulliver's softer tone and defensive justification show his emotional capitulation, though the words are brief.
enrichment.best_quote: I've allays done what I could for you.
enrichment.summary: Mr Tulliver addresses his sister with new softness, defending himself by recalling his past support for her.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver Shows His Weaker Side
text:
“I’m not denying that, brother, and I’m noways
ungrateful,” said poor Mrs Moss, too fagged by toil and children to have
strength left for any pride. “But here’s the father. What a while
you’ve been, Moss!”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mrs Moss's grateful and weary reply is poignant but brief and routine.
enrichment.summary: Mrs Moss assures her brother she is grateful and not denying his help, noting her exhaustion from toil and children, then announces Mr Moss's approach.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver Shows His Weaker Side
text:
“While, do you call it?” said Mr Moss, feeling out of breath and
injured. “I’ve been running all the way. Won’t you
’light, Mr Tulliver?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: A routine greeting with Mr Moss's complaint about exertion; minimal character or plot significance.
enrichment.summary: Mr Moss arrives breathless from running and asks if Mr Tulliver will dismount.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver Shows His Weaker Side
text:
“Well, I’ll just get down and have a bit o’ talk with you in
the garden,” said Mr Tulliver, thinking that he should be more likely to
show a due spirit of resolve if his sister were not present.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mr Tulliver's decision to dismount for a garden conversation shows his shift toward discussion, though the narration notes his strategic reasoning.
enrichment.best_quote: Let him keep in his saddle and speak from that height, above the level of pleading eyes.
enrichment.summary: Mr Tulliver dismounts and proposes a private conversation with Mr Moss in the garden, believing discussion away from his sister will help him maintain firmness.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver Shows His Weaker Side
text:
He got down, and passed with Mr Moss into the garden, toward an old yew-tree
arbour, while his sister stood tapping her baby on the back and looking
wistfully after them.

enrichment.interest_rationale: A transition to the garden scene with a small atmospheric touch of Mrs Moss's melancholy maternal waiting.
enrichment.summary: Mr Tulliver and Mr Moss walk toward the yew-tree arbour while Mrs Moss remains behind, rocking her baby and looking after them wistfully.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver Shows His Weaker Side
text:
Their entrance into the yew-tree arbour surprised several fowls that were
recreating themselves by scratching deep holes in the dusty ground, and at once
took flight with much pother and cackling. Mr Tulliver sat down on the bench,
and tapping the ground curiously here and there with his stick, as if he
suspected some hollowness, opened the conversation by observing, with something
like a snarl in his tone,—

enrichment.interest_rationale: The yew-tree arbour scene opens with atmospheric detail and Mr Tulliver's hostile demeanor signalled through his snarling tone.
enrichment.summary: The two men enter the yew-tree arbour, startling fowls; Mr Tulliver sits and begins probing the ground suspiciously before speaking with a snarl.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver Shows His Weaker Side
text:
“Why, you’ve got wheat again in that Corner Close, I see; and never
a bit o’ dressing on it. You’ll do no good with it this
year.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mr Tulliver begins criticizing Moss's farming practices in a hostile manner to ease into the financial confrontation.
enrichment.summary: Mr Tulliver opens the conversation by criticizing Moss's farming of the Corner Close, claiming it will yield no good without proper dressing.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver Shows His Weaker Side
text:
Mr Moss, who, when he married Miss Tulliver, had been regarded as the buck of
Basset, now wore a beard nearly a week old, and had the depressed, unexpectant
air of a machine-horse. He answered in a patient-grumbling tone, “Why,
poor farmers like me must do as they can; they must leave it to them as have
got money to play with, to put half as much into the ground as they mean to get
out of it.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mr Moss's depressed acceptance and defensive explanation reveal his unfortunate circumstances and worn character.
enrichment.best_quote: poor farmers like me must do as they can; they must leave it to them as have got money to play with, to put half as much into the ground as they mean to get out of it.
enrichment.summary: Mr Moss responds with resigned complaint, noting that poor farmers must make do while the wealthy can invest capital; the narrator describes his deteriorated appearance since his marriage.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver Shows His Weaker Side
text:
“I don’t know who should have money to play with, if it isn’t
them as can borrow money without paying interest,” said Mr Tulliver, who
wished to get into a slight quarrel; it was the most natural and easy
introduction to calling in money.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mr Tulliver's barbed remark initiates the quarrel he desires, revealing his poor motivation and the move toward calling in the debt.
enrichment.best_quote: I don't know who should have money to play with, if it isn't them as can borrow money without paying interest.
enrichment.summary: Mr Tulliver makes a pointed comment about those who borrow without paying interest, setting up the financial confrontation.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver Shows His Weaker Side
text:
“I know I’m behind with the interest,” said Mr Moss,
“but I was so unlucky wi’ the wool last year; and what with the
Missis being laid up so, things have gone awk’arder nor usual.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mr Moss's admission and excuses establish his defensiveness without adding much narrative depth.
enrichment.summary: Mr Moss admits to being behind on interest payments, blaming poor wool markets and his wife's illness.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver Shows His Weaker Side
text:
“Ay,” snarled Mr Tulliver, “there’s folks as things
’ull allays go awk’ard with; empty sacks ’ull never stand
upright.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mr Tulliver's contemptuous proverb about empty sacks, though colorful, is a familiar rhetorical flourish in his bullying approach.
enrichment.best_quote: empty sacks 'ull never stand upright.
enrichment.summary: Mr Tulliver delivers a snarling proverb, suggesting that the incompetent (empty sacks) will always struggle.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver Shows His Weaker Side
text:
“Well, I don’t know what fault you’ve got to find wi’
me, Mr Tulliver,” said Mr Moss, deprecatingly; “I know there
isn’t a day-labourer works harder.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mr Moss's mild protest is routine defensive dialogue.
enrichment.summary: Mr Moss protests that he works hard and cannot be blamed for his circumstances.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver Shows His Weaker Side
text:
“What’s the use o’ that,” said Mr Tulliver, sharply,
“when a man marries, and’s got no capital to work his farm but his
wife’s bit o’ fortin? I was against it from the first; but
you’d neither of you listen to me. And I can’t lie out o’ my
money any longer, for I’ve got to pay five hundred o’ Mrs
Glegg’s, and there’ll be Tom an expense to me. I should find myself
short, even saying I’d got back all as is my own. You must look about and
see how you can pay me the three hundred pound.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: The climax of the financial demand: Mr Tulliver's harsh ultimatum reveals his desperation and explains the total financial situation (five hundred to Mrs Glegg, three hundred owed by Moss, Tom's school expense).
enrichment.best_quote: I can't lie out o' my money any longer, for I've got to pay five hundred o' Mrs Glegg's, and there'll be Tom an expense to me. I should find myself short, even saying I'd got back all as is my own.
enrichment.summary: Mr Tulliver delivers his harsh demand for repayment of the three-hundred-pound loan, explaining his own financial strain from Mrs Glegg's loan and Tom's school expenses.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver Shows His Weaker Side
text:
“Well, if that’s what you mean,” said Mr Moss, looking
blankly before him, “we’d better be sold up, and ha’ done
with it; I must part wi’ every head o’ stock I’ve got, to pay
you and the landlord too.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mr Moss's desperate response reveals the catastrophic impact of the demand and the tragic position of poor farmers.
enrichment.best_quote: we'd better be sold up, and ha' done with it; I must part wi' every head o' stock I've got, to pay you and the landlord too.
enrichment.summary: Mr Moss responds with despair, saying he would have to liquidate all his livestock to meet both Mr Tulliver's demand and his landlord's claims.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver Shows His Weaker Side
text:
Poor relations are undeniably irritating,—their existence is so entirely
uncalled for on our part, and they are almost always very faulty people. Mr
Tulliver had succeeded in getting quite as much irritated with Mr Moss as he
had desired, and he was able to say angrily, rising from his seat,—

enrichment.interest_rationale: The narrator's commentary on poor relations provides sharp ironic insight into middle-class callousness; Mr Tulliver achieves his desired irritation and rises to exit.
enrichment.best_quote: Poor relations are undeniably irritating,—their existence is so entirely uncalled for on our part, and they are almost always very faulty people.
enrichment.summary: The narrator reflects on the universal irritation poor relations provoke in the well-to-do, noting Mr Tulliver has succeeded in achieving the desired state of anger.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver Shows His Weaker Side
text:
“Well, you must do as you can.  I  can’t find money for
everybody else as well as myself. I must look to my own business and my own
family. I can’t lie out o’ my money any longer. You must raise it
as quick as you can.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mr Tulliver's final harsh statement in the arbour asserts his prioritisation of self-interest and family over his sister's welfare.
enrichment.best_quote: I can't find money for everybody else as well as myself. I must look to my own business and my own family.
enrichment.summary: Mr Tulliver angrily declares he cannot support everyone and must prioritize his own family's interests, demanding rapid repayment.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver Shows His Weaker Side
text:
Mr Tulliver walked abruptly out of the arbour as he uttered the last sentence,
and, without looking round at Mr Moss, went on to the kitchen door, where the
eldest boy was holding his horse, and his sister was waiting in a state of
wondering alarm, which was not without its alleviations, for baby was making
pleasant gurgling sounds, and performing a great deal of finger practice on the
faded face. Mrs Moss had eight children, but could never overcome her regret
that the twins had not lived. Mr Moss thought their removal was not without
its consolations. “Won’t you come in, brother?” she said,
looking anxiously at her husband, who was walking slowly up, while Mr Tulliver
had his foot already in the stirrup.

enrichment.interest_rationale: The return to the kitchen provides a touching tableau of Mrs Moss's maternal tenderness amid family crisis, and prepares for the reversal.
enrichment.summary: Mr Tulliver departs the arbour, encounters his sister waiting with her baby at the kitchen door in anxious alarm; the narrator notes her grief over the twins' death and Mr Moss's indifference.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver Shows His Weaker Side
text:
“No, no; good-by,” said he, turning his horse’s head, and
riding away.

enrichment.interest_rationale: A minimal farewell before the reversal.
enrichment.summary: Mr Tulliver declines further invitation and turns his horse to leave.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver Shows His Weaker Side
text:
No man could feel more resolute till he got outside the yard gate, and a little
way along the deep-rutted lane; but before he reached the next turning, which
would take him out of sight of the dilapidated farm-buildings, he appeared to
be smitten by some sudden thought. He checked his horse, and made it stand
still in the same spot for two or three minutes, during which he turned his
head from side to side in a melancholy way, as if he were looking at some
painful object on more sides than one. Evidently, after his fit of promptitude,
Mr Tulliver was relapsing into the sense that this is a puzzling world. He
turned his horse, and rode slowly back, giving vent to the climax of feeling
which had determined this movement by saying aloud, as he struck his horse,
“Poor little wench! she’ll have nobody but Tom, belike, when
I’m gone.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: The emotional and thematic climax of the chapter: Mr Tulliver's private reversal on the lane, his melancholic meditation on Maggie's future without him, and his anguished exclamation reveal his deepest paternal anxiety and moral confusion, undoing his harsh decision.
enrichment.best_quote: Poor little wench! she'll have nobody but Tom, belike, when I'm gone.
enrichment.summary: As Mr Tulliver rides away, he is suddenly struck by painful reflection about Maggie's vulnerability and future dependence on Tom after his death, causing him to turn his horse back with sorrow and determination.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver Shows His Weaker Side
text:
Mr Tulliver’s return into the yard was descried by several young Mosses,
who immediately ran in with the exciting news to their mother, so that Mrs
Moss was again on the door-step when her brother rode up. She had been crying,
but was rocking baby to sleep in her arms now, and made no ostentatious show of
sorrow as her brother looked at her, but merely said:

enrichment.interest_rationale: A brief narrative transition showing Mrs Moss's quiet dignity and maternal focus as she awaits her brother's return.
enrichment.summary: Young Mosses announce their uncle's return, and Mrs Moss appears at the door, having composed herself despite her tears.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver Shows His Weaker Side
text:
“The father’s gone to the field, again, if you want him,
brother.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: A minimal announcement with no distinctive content.
enrichment.summary: Mrs Moss offers to fetch her husband from the field.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver Shows His Weaker Side
text:
“No, Gritty, no,” said Mr Tulliver, in a gentle tone.
“Don’t you fret,—that’s all,—I’ll make a
shift without the money a bit, only you must be as clever and contriving as you
can.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: The emotional resolution: Mr Tulliver's complete reversal and tender reassurance to his sister, his release of the debt demand, expressed in gentle dialect and affection—a transformative moment.
enrichment.best_quote: Don't you fret,—that's all,—I'll make a shift without the money a bit, only you must be as clever and contriving as you can.
enrichment.summary: Mr Tulliver tells his sister not to worry, assuring her he will manage without the debt repayment if she remains resourceful and frugal.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver Shows His Weaker Side
text:
Mrs Moss’s tears came again at this unexpected kindness, and she could
say nothing.

enrichment.interest_rationale: A minimal emotional response; purely functional.
enrichment.summary: Mrs Moss's tears return in gratitude, leaving her speechless.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver Shows His Weaker Side
text:
“Come, come!—the little wench shall come and see you. I’ll
bring her and Tom some day before he goes to school. You mustn’t fret.
I’ll allays be a good brother to you.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mr Tulliver's generous promise to bring the children for a visit and his affirmation of brotherly love provide warm resolution.
enrichment.best_quote: the little wench shall come and see you. I'll bring her and Tom some day before he goes to school.
enrichment.summary: Mr Tulliver promises to bring Maggie and Tom to visit their aunt, and assures Mrs Moss of his permanent good will.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver Shows His Weaker Side
text:
“Thank you for that word, brother,” said Mrs Moss, drying her
tears; then turning to Lizzy, she said, “Run now, and fetch the coloured
egg for cousin Maggie.” Lizzy ran in, and quickly reappeared with a small
paper parcel.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mrs Moss recovers her voice to thank him and instructs Lizzy to fetch a gift, showing maternal tenderness and gratitude.
enrichment.summary: Mrs Moss thanks her brother and instructs her daughter to fetch a coloured egg prepared for Maggie.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver Shows His Weaker Side

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mrs Moss describes the gift with modest pride, a small touching detail of maternal love and connection.
enrichment.summary: Mrs Moss explains the egg was specially prepared and coloured for Maggie, and asks her brother to carry it for her.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver Shows His Weaker Side
text:
“Ay, ay,” said Mr Tulliver, putting it carefully in his side
pocket. “Good-by.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: A perfunctory farewell with Mr Tulliver securing the gift.
enrichment.summary: Mr Tulliver carefully places the egg in his pocket and departs.

chapter_title: Mr Tulliver Shows His Weaker Side
text:
And so the respectable miller returned along the Basset lanes rather more
puzzled than before as to ways and means, but still with the sense of a danger
escaped. It had come across his mind that if he were hard upon his sister, it
might somehow tend to make Tom hard upon Maggie at some distant day, when her
father was no longer there to take her part; for simple people, like our friend
Mr Tulliver, are apt to clothe unimpeachable feelings in erroneous ideas, and
this was his confused way of explaining to himself that his love and anxiety
for “the little wench” had given him a new sensibility toward his
sister.

enrichment.interest_rationale: The concluding narrative reflection explains Mr Tulliver's psychological reconciliation through his confused but genuine love for Maggie, using the metaphor of transferred maternal anxiety to understand his moral reversal and ambivalence.
enrichment.best_quote: simple people, like our friend Mr Tulliver, are apt to clothe unimpeachable feelings in erroneous ideas, and this was his confused way of explaining to himself that his love and anxiety for 'the little wench' had given him a new sensibility toward his sister.
enrichment.summary: The narrator reflects that Mr Tulliver, though puzzled about finances, feels a sense of danger escaped; his love for Maggie has granted him new sympathy for his sister, though expressed through confused reasoning about protecting Maggie's future.

text:
While the possible troubles of Maggie’s future were occupying her
father’s mind, she herself was tasting only the bitterness of the
present. Childhood has no forebodings; but then, it is soothed by no memories
of outlived sorrow.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Philosophical opening on childhood suffering that establishes thematic ground for the chapter's emotional arc.
enrichment.best_quote: Childhood has no forebodings; but then, it is soothed by no memories of outlived sorrow.
enrichment.summary: The narrator reflects on childhood's inability to foresee future troubles, yet its lack of comfort from past sorrows.

text:
The fact was, the day had begun ill with Maggie. The pleasure of having Lucy to
look at, and the prospect of the afternoon visit to Garum Firs, where she would
hear uncle Pullet’s musical box, had been marred as early as eleven
o’clock by the advent of the hair-dresser from St Ogg’s, who had
spoken in the severest terms of the condition in which he had found her hair,
holding up one jagged lock after another and saying, “See here! tut, tut,
tut!” in a tone of mingled disgust and pity, which to Maggie’s
imagination was equivalent to the strongest expression of public opinion. Mr
Rappit, the hair-dresser, with his well-anointed coronal locks tending wavily
upward, like the simulated pyramid of flame on a monumental urn, seemed to her
at that moment the most formidable of her contemporaries, into whose street at
St Ogg’s she would carefully refrain from entering through the rest of
her life.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Comic-gothic portrait of Maggie's mortification at the hair-dresser's visit, establishing her emotional vulnerability and social anxiety with vivid, amusing detail.
enrichment.best_quote: See here! tut, tut, tut!
enrichment.summary: Maggie's day begins badly when a hair-dresser from St Ogg's criticises the condition of her hair in harsh terms, making her fear public judgment and vowing to avoid his street.

text:
Moreover, the preparation for a visit being always a serious affair in the
Dodson family, Martha was enjoined to have Mrs Tulliver’s room ready an
hour earlier than usual, that the laying out of the best clothes might not be
deferred till the last moment, as was sometimes the case in families of lax
views, where the ribbon-strings were never rolled up, where there was little or
no wrapping in silver paper, and where the sense that the Sunday clothes could
be got at quite easily produced no shock to the mind. Already, at twelve
o’clock, Mrs Tulliver had on her visiting costume, with a protective
apparatus of brown holland, as if she had been a piece of satin furniture in
danger of flies; Maggie was frowning and twisting her shoulders, that she might
if possible shrink away from the prickliest of tuckers, while her mother was
remonstrating, “Don’t, Maggie, my dear; don’t make yourself
so ugly!” and Tom’s cheeks were looking particularly brilliant as a
relief to his best blue suit, which he wore with becoming calmness, having,
after a little wrangling, effected what was always the one point of interest to
him in his toilet: he had transferred all the contents of his everyday pockets
to those actually in wear.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Satirical depiction of Dodson family respectability rituals and clothing anxiety; establishes class values but becomes somewhat repetitive.
enrichment.summary: The Tulliver household prepares elaborately for their visit to Garum Firs; Mrs Tulliver dons protective brown holland, Maggie fusses against her tucker, and Tom carefully transfers his pocket contents.

text:
As for Lucy, she was just as pretty and neat as she had been yesterday; no
accidents ever happened to her clothes, and she was never uncomfortable in
them, so that she looked with wondering pity at Maggie, pouting and writhing
under the exasperating tucker. Maggie would certainly have torn it off, if she
had not been checked by the remembrance of her recent humiliation about her
hair; as it was, she confined herself to fretting and twisting, and behaving
peevishly about the card-houses which they were allowed to build till dinner,
as a suitable amusement for boys and girls in their best clothes. Tom could
build perfect pyramids of houses; but Maggie’s would never bear the
laying on the roof. It was always so with the things that Maggie made; and Tom
had deduced the conclusion that no girls could ever make anything. But it
happened that Lucy proved wonderfully clever at building; she handled the cards
so lightly, and moved so gently, that Tom condescended to admire her houses as
well as his own, the more readily because she had asked him to teach her.
Maggie, too, would have admired Lucy’s houses, and would have given up
her own unsuccessful building to contemplate them, without ill temper, if her
tucker had not made her peevish, and if Tom had not inconsiderately laughed
when her houses fell, and told her she was “a stupid.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Contrasts Maggie's clumsiness with Lucy's grace and Tom's condescension toward girls; reinforces gender themes but covers familiar ground.
enrichment.summary: While Lucy builds perfect card-houses and Tom admires her, Maggie's constructions collapse; Tom concludes that no girls can make anything, and laughs at her failure.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Simple dialogue line that reveals Maggie's defensiveness but lacks particular force or complexity.
enrichment.summary: Maggie responds angrily to Tom's laughter, defending her intelligence.

text:
“Oh, I dare say, Miss Spitfire! I’d never be such a cross thing as
you, making faces like that. Lucy doesn’t do so. I like Lucy better than
you;  I  wish Lucy was  my  sister.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Tom's taunting response is characteristic but brief; escalates the quarrel without substantial complexity.
enrichment.summary: Tom mocks Maggie as a cross and spitfire, preferring Lucy, who does not make faces.

text:
“Then it’s very wicked and cruel of you to wish so,” said
Maggie, starting up hurriedly from her place on the floor, and upsetting
Tom’s wonderful pagoda. She really did not mean it, but the
circumstantial evidence was against her, and Tom turned white with anger, but
said nothing; he would have struck her, only he knew it was cowardly to strike
a girl, and Tom Tulliver was quite determined he would never do anything
cowardly.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Maggie's destructive impulse (overturning Tom's pagoda) and the narrator's commentary on Tom's honour code create a turning point with psychological depth.
enrichment.summary: Maggie, distressed by Tom's wish that Lucy were his sister, destroys his card pagoda; Tom wants to strike her but restrains himself, believing it cowardly.

text:
Maggie stood in dismay and terror, while Tom got up from the floor and walked
away, pale, from the scattered ruins of his pagoda, and Lucy looked on mutely,
like a kitten pausing from its lapping.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Brief scene of aftermath; emotionally charged but thin on substance.
enrichment.summary: Maggie stands in terror while Tom walks away from his destroyed pagoda; Lucy watches silently.

text:
“Oh, Tom,” said Maggie, at last, going half-way toward him,
“I didn’t mean to knock it down, indeed, indeed I
didn’t.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Maggie's brief apology is routine connective dialogue with minimal dramatic or emotional weight.
enrichment.summary: Maggie attempts to apologise to Tom, claiming she did not mean to knock down his pagoda.

text:
Tom took no notice of her, but took, instead, two or three hard peas out of his
pocket, and shot them with his thumbnail against the window, vaguely at first,
but presently with the distinct aim of hitting a superannuated blue-bottle
which was exposing its imbecility in the spring sunshine, clearly against the
views of Nature, who had provided Tom and the peas for the speedy destruction
of this weak individual.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Tom's distraction with shooting peas at a fly is comic and reveals his boyish nature; the narrator's philosophical aside on Nature and mastery is playful.
enrichment.summary: Tom ignores Maggie and instead shoots peas with his thumbnail at a blue-bottle fly in the window, pursuing it with determined aim.

text:
Thus the morning had been made heavy to Maggie, and Tom’s persistent
coldness to her all through their walk spoiled the fresh air and sunshine for
her. He called Lucy to look at the half-built bird’s nest without caring
to show it Maggie, and peeled a willow switch for Lucy and himself, without
offering one to Maggie. Lucy had said, “Maggie, shouldn’t
 you  like one?” but Tom was deaf.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Depicts Tom's persistent coldness toward Maggie during their walk to Garum Firs; emotionally affecting and shows sibling dynamics, though somewhat repetitive of the earlier quarrel.
enrichment.summary: Tom remains coldly distant to Maggie throughout their walk, showing Lucy the bird's nest and peeling willow switches for himself and Lucy, but not for Maggie.

text:
Still, the sight of the peacock opportunely spreading his tail on the stackyard
wall, just as they reached Garum Firs, was enough to divert the mind
temporarily from personal grievances. And this was only the beginning of
beautiful sights at Garum Firs. All the farmyard life was wonderful
there,—bantams, speckled and top-knotted; Friesland hens, with their
feathers all turned the wrong way; Guinea-fowls that flew and screamed and
dropped their pretty spotted feathers; pouter-pigeons and a tame magpie; nay, a
goat, and a wonderful brindled dog, half mastiff, half bull-dog, as large as a
lion. Then there were white railings and white gates all about, and glittering
weathercocks of various design, and garden-walks paved with pebbles in
beautiful patterns,—nothing was quite common at Garum Firs; and Tom
thought that the unusual size of the toads there was simply due to the general
unusualness which characterised uncle Pullet’s possessions as a gentleman
farmer. Toads who paid rent were naturally leaner. As for the house, it was not
less remarkable; it had a receding centre, and two wings with battlemented
turrets, and was covered with glittering white stucco.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Vivid, whimsical description of Garum Firs' farmyard and gardens; establishes Uncle Pullet's status and introduces the estate as a wonderland for the children.
enrichment.summary: The narrator describes the extraordinary farmyard and gardens of Garum Firs, with exotic animals, white railings, patterned walks, and a striking stuccoed house with turrets, all suggesting Uncle Pullet's unusual status as a gentleman farmer.

text:
Uncle Pullet had seen the expected party approaching from the window, and made
haste to unbar and unchain the front door, kept always in this fortified
condition from fear of tramps, who might be supposed to know of the glass case
of stuffed birds in the hall, and to contemplate rushing in and carrying it
away on their heads. Aunt Pullet, too, appeared at the doorway, and as soon as
her sister was within hearing said, “Stop the children, for God’s
sake! Bessy; don’t let ’em come up the door-steps; Sally’s
bringing the old mat and the duster, to rub their shoes.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Comic scene of Uncle Pullet's anxious hospitality and house protocols; establishes atmosphere but lacks substantial interest.
enrichment.summary: Uncle Pullet admits the family; Aunt Pullet immediately instructs them to have their shoes wiped on a mat before entering, fearing tramps might steal the stuffed birds in the hall.

text:
Mrs Pullet’s front-door mats were by no means intended to wipe shoes on;
the very scraper had a deputy to do its dirty work. Tom rebelled particularly
against this shoewiping, which he always considered in the light of an
indignity to his sex. He felt it as the beginning of the disagreeables incident
to a visit at aunt Pullet’s, where he had once been compelled to sit with
towels wrapped round his boots; a fact which may serve to correct the too hasty
conclusion that a visit to Garum Firs must have been a great treat to a young
gentleman fond of animals,—fond, that is, of throwing stones at them.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Tom's rebellion against shoe-wiping ceremonies and memory of boot-wrapping; reveals his gender consciousness and satirises the Pullet household's obsessive propriety.
enrichment.summary: Tom dislikes the shoe-wiping ritual as beneath his masculine dignity, remembering a previous visit when he was made to sit with towels wrapped around his boots.

text:
The next disagreeable was confined to his feminine companions; it was the
mounting of the polished oak stairs, which had very handsome carpets rolled up
and laid by in a spare bedroom, so that the ascent of these glossy steps might
have served, in barbarous times, as a trial by ordeal from which none but the
most spotless virtue could have come off with unbroken limbs. Sophy’s
weakness about these polished stairs was always a subject of bitter
remonstrance on Mrs Glegg’s part; but Mrs Tulliver ventured on no
comment, only thinking to herself it was a mercy when she and the children were
safe on the landing.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Describes the hazard of polished stairs for the girls; mildly comic but brief and somewhat routine.
enrichment.summary: The polished oak stairs at Garum Firs present a dangerous ascent for the girls; Mrs Tulliver is relieved when they reach the landing safely, while Mrs Glegg criticises Sophy Pullet's weakness on the stairs.

text:
“Mrs Gray has sent home my new bonnet, Bessy,” said Mrs Pullet,
in a pathetic tone, as Mrs Tulliver adjusted her cap.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Minimal opening line to the bonnet discussion; pure connective dialogue.
enrichment.summary: Mrs Pullet mentions that Mrs Gray has sent home her new bonnet.

text:
“Has she, sister?” said Mrs Tulliver, with an air of much
interest. “And how do you like it?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Routine response from Mrs Tulliver; bare connective dialogue.
enrichment.summary: Mrs Tulliver expresses interest in seeing the bonnet.

text:
“It’s apt to make a mess with clothes, taking ’em out and
putting ’em in again,” said Mrs Pullet, drawing a bunch of keys
from her pocket and looking at them earnestly, “but it ’ud be a
pity for you to go away without seeing it. There’s no knowing what may
happen.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mrs Pullet's cryptic remarks about the bonnet's care and mortality suggestion hint at the peculiar solemnity she brings to her possessions.
enrichment.best_quote: There's no knowing what may happen.
enrichment.summary: Mrs Pullet cryptically warns that the bonnet causes mess and may never be seen again, suggesting some unspoken doom.

text:
Mrs Pullet shook her head slowly at this last serious consideration, which
determined her to single out a particular key.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Minimal action line; routine transition.
enrichment.summary: Mrs Pullet shakes her head and selects a key from her pocket.

text:
“I’m afraid it’ll be troublesome to you getting it out,
sister,” said Mrs Tulliver; “but I  should  like to see what
sort of a crown she’s made you.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Routine dialogue continuing the bonnet preparations.
enrichment.summary: Mrs Tulliver politely expresses concern about troubling her sister but wishes to see the bonnet's crown.

text:
Mrs Pullet rose with a melancholy air and unlocked one wing of a very bright
wardrobe, where you may have hastily supposed she would find a new bonnet. Not
at all. Such a supposition could only have arisen from a too superficial
acquaintance with the habits of the Dodson family. In this wardrobe Mrs Pullet
was seeking something small enough to be hidden among layers of linen,—it
was a door-key.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Comic revelation that the wardrobe contains not the bonnet but a door-key; exemplifies the Dodson family's peculiar rituals and the narrator's amused irony about their habits.
enrichment.best_quote: Such a supposition could only have arisen from a too superficial acquaintance with the habits of the Dodson family.
enrichment.summary: When Mrs Pullet opens the wardrobe, she does not retrieve the bonnet but a small door-key hidden among layers of linen, revealing the Dodsons' elaborate storage practices.

text: “You must come with me into the best room,” said Mrs Pullet.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Minimal connective dialogue.
enrichment.summary: Mrs Pullet invites her sister to the best room.

text:
“May the children come too, sister?” inquired Mrs Tulliver, who
saw that Maggie and Lucy were looking rather eager.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Routine enquiry from Mrs Tulliver; bare connective dialogue.
enrichment.summary: Mrs Tulliver asks if the children may come to the best room.

text:
“Well,” said aunt Pullet, reflectively, “it’ll perhaps
be safer for ’em to come; they’ll be touching something if we leave
’em behind.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mrs Pullet's logic for allowing the children (to prevent mischief) is mildly comic but brief.
enrichment.summary: Aunt Pullet agrees it is safer to let the children come, as they might touch something if left behind.

text:
So they went in procession along the bright and slippery corridor, dimly
lighted by the semi-lunar top of the window which rose above the closed
shutter; it was really quite solemn. Aunt Pullet paused and unlocked a door
which opened on something still more solemn than the passage,—a darkened
room, in which the outer light, entering feebly, showed what looked like the
corpses of furniture in white shrouds. Everything that was not shrouded stood
with its legs upward. Lucy laid hold of Maggie’s frock, and
Maggie’s heart beat rapidly.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Gothic, atmospheric passage with vivid imagery of the darkened best room; creates genuine suspense and eerie mood while advancing the ceremonial bonnet-viewing.
enrichment.best_quote: a darkened room, in which the outer light, entering feebly, showed what looked like the corpses of furniture in white shrouds.
enrichment.summary: The group processes along a dim corridor and enters a darkened best room where furniture lies under white shrouds like corpses; Lucy grabs Maggie's frock in fear.

text:
Aunt Pullet half-opened the shutter and then unlocked the wardrobe, with a
melancholy deliberateness which was quite in keeping with the funereal
solemnity of the scene. The delicious scent of rose-leaves that issued from the
wardrobe made the process of taking out sheet after sheet of silver paper quite
pleasant to assist at, though the sight of the bonnet at last was an anticlimax
to Maggie, who would have preferred something more strikingly preternatural.
But few things could have been more impressive to Mrs Tulliver. She looked all
round it in silence for some moments, and then said emphatically, “Well,
sister, I’ll never speak against the full crowns again!”

enrichment.interest_rationale: The bonnet-viewing combines Gothic ceremony with mundane domestic detail; Mrs Pullet's deliberateness and Mrs Tulliver's impressed reaction reveal class anxiety and ritual significance.
enrichment.summary: Mrs Pullet opens the wardrobe; the scent of rose-leaves emerges as she unwraps layer after layer of silver paper to reveal the bonnet, which disappoints Maggie but impresses Mrs Tulliver.

text:
It was a great concession, and Mrs Pullet felt it; she felt something was due
to it.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Brief line acknowledging Mrs Tulliver's compliment; lacks substantial weight.
enrichment.summary: Mrs Pullet feels gratified by her sister's admiration and believes a response is warranted.

text:
“You’d like to see it on, sister?” she said sadly.
“I’ll open the shutter a bit further.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Routine transition dialogue.
enrichment.summary: Mrs Pullet offers to display the bonnet on her head and to adjust the shutter light.

text:
“Well, if you don’t mind taking off your cap, sister,” said
Mrs Tulliver.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Routine connective dialogue.
enrichment.summary: Mrs Tulliver asks if Mrs Pullet would remove her cap before trying on the bonnet.

text:
Mrs Pullet took off her cap, displaying the brown silk scalp with a jutting
promontory of curls which was common to the more mature and judicious women of
those times, and placing the bonnet on her head, turned slowly round, like a
draper’s lay-figure, that Mrs Tulliver might miss no point of view.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Comic physical description of Mrs Pullet; captures her mannered presentation and the absurdity of the bonnet ceremony.
enrichment.summary: Mrs Pullet removes her cap, revealing the brown silk scalp with curls, then slowly turns while wearing the bonnet so Mrs Tulliver can view it from all angles.

text:
“I’ve sometimes thought there’s a loop too much o’
ribbon on this left side, sister; what do you think?” said Mrs Pullet.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mrs Pullet's minor doubt about ribbon placement; minimal substance.
enrichment.summary: Mrs Pullet wonders if there is too much ribbon on the left side of the bonnet.

text:
Mrs Tulliver looked earnestly at the point indicated, and turned her head on
one side. “Well, I think it’s best as it is; if you meddled with
it, sister, you might repent.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mrs Tulliver's reassuring response; routine dialogue.
enrichment.summary: Mrs Tulliver advises against altering the ribbon lest Mrs Pullet come to regret the change.

text:
“That’s true,” said aunt Pullet, taking off the bonnet and
looking at it contemplatively.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mrs Pullet's acceptance is routine and unmemorable.

long upstairs. With Tom the interval had seemed still longer, for he had been

“Well, young sir, what do you learn at school?” was a standing
question with uncle Pullet; whereupon Tom always looked sheepish, rubbed his
hands across his face, and answered, “I don’t know.” It was
altogether so embarrassing to be seated  tête-à-tête  with uncle Pullet,
that Tom could not even look at the prints on the walls, or the flycages, or
the wonderful flower-pots; he saw nothing but his uncle’s gaiters. Not
that Tom was in awe of his uncle’s mental superiority; indeed, he had
made up his mind that he didn’t want to be a gentleman farmer, because he
shouldn’t like to be such a thin-legged, silly fellow as his uncle
Pullet,—a molly-coddle, in fact. A boy’s sheepishness is by no
means a sign of overmastering reverence; and while you are making encouraging
advances to him under the idea that he is overwhelmed by a sense of your age
and wisdom, ten to one he is thinking you extremely queer. The only consolation
I can suggest to you is, that the Greek boys probably thought the same of
Aristotle. It is only when you have mastered a restive horse, or thrashed a
drayman, or have got a gun in your hand, that these shy juniors feel you to be
a truly admirable and enviable character. At least, I am quite sure of Tom
Tulliver’s sentiments on these points. In very tender years, when he
still wore a lace border under his outdoor cap, he was often observed peeping
through the bars of a gate and making minatory gestures with his small
forefinger while he scolded the sheep with an inarticulate burr, intended to
strike terror into their astonished minds; indicating thus early that desire
for mastery over the inferior animals, wild and domestic, including
cockchafers, neighbours’ dogs, and small sisters, which in all ages has
been an attribute of so much promise for the fortunes of our race. Now, Mr
Pullet never rode anything taller than a low pony, and was the least predatory
of men, considering firearms dangerous, as apt to go off of themselves by
nobody’s particular desire. So that Tom was not without strong reasons
when, in confidential talk with a chum, he had described uncle Pullet as a
nincompoop, taking care at the same time to observe that he was a very
“rich fellow.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Extended philosophical digression on boyish psychology and Tom's contempt for Uncle Pullet despite social awkwardness; reveals character through the narrator's ironic commentary.
enrichment.best_quote: A boy's sheepishness is by no means a sign of overmastering reverence
enrichment.summary: The narrator explains that Tom's shy discomfort with Uncle Pullet masks contempt; Tom admires men of action (horsemasters, fighters, gunmen) not quiet gentlemen. Tom regards his uncle as a foolish milksop.

rather a pity to eat it; but Tom, watching his opportunity while the elders

furtively. As for Maggie, becoming fascinated, as usual, by a print of Ulysses
and Nausicaa, which uncle Pullet had bought as a “pretty Scripture
thing,” she presently let fall her cake, and in an unlucky movement
crushed it beneath her foot,—a source of so much agitation to aunt Pullet
and conscious disgrace to Maggie, that she began to despair of hearing the
musical snuff-box to-day, till, after some reflection, it occurred to her that
Lucy was in high favour enough to venture on asking for a tune. So she whispered
to Lucy; and Lucy, who always did what she was desired to do, went up quietly

Lucy thought it was by reason of some exceptional talent in uncle Pullet that

that light by the majority of his neighbours in Garum. Mr Pullet had

which tune it was going to play beforehand; altogether the possession of this
unique “piece of music” was a proof that Mr Pullet’s
character was not of that entire nullity which might otherwise have been
attributed to it. But uncle Pullet, when entreated to exhibit his
accomplishment, never depreciated it by a too ready consent. “We’ll
see about it,” was the answer he always gave, carefully abstaining from
any sign of compliance till a suitable number of minutes had passed. Uncle
Pullet had a programme for all great social occasions, and in this way fenced
himself in from much painful confusion and perplexing freedom of will.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Aunt Pullet's principled position that Mr Tulliver should apologize first; shows her respect for social propriety despite her sympathy.
enrichment.summary: Aunt Pullet maintains that Mr Tulliver should apologize to Mrs Glegg for his rash speech, especially given his indebtedness to her.

“It’s no use talking o’ that,” said poor Mrs Tulliver,
almost peevishly. “If I was to go down on my bare knees on the gravel to
Tulliver, he’d never humble himself.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mrs Tulliver's hopeless statement that Mr Tulliver will not humble himself; establishes his pride as a central obstacle.
enrichment.summary: Mrs Tulliver despairs that Mr Tulliver will never humble himself, however much she begs him to do so.

“Well, you can’t expect me to persuade  Jane  to beg
pardon,” said Mrs Pullet. “Her temper’s beyond everything;
it’s well if it doesn’t carry her off her mind, though there never
 was  any of our family went to a madhouse.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Aunt Pullet's assessment that Mrs Glegg's temper is beyond remedy; brief and somewhat predictable.
enrichment.summary: Aunt Pullet observes that Mrs Glegg's temper is so bad that it might drive her mad, though the family has no history of madness.

text:
“I’m not thinking of her begging pardon,” said Mrs Tulliver.
“But if she’d just take no notice, and not call her money in; as
it’s not so much for one sister to ask of another; time ’ud mend
things, and Tulliver ’ud forget all about it, and they’d be friends
again.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mrs Tulliver clarifies her modest hope that Mrs Glegg will simply not demand repayment; shows her pragmatic desperation.
enrichment.summary: Mrs Tulliver hopes only that Mrs Glegg will ignore the quarrel and not call in her loan, giving time for the conflict to fade.

determination to pay in the five hundred pounds; at least such a determination

enrichment.interest_rationale: Narrator reveals that Mrs Tulliver is unaware of Mr Tulliver's determination to repay the loan; establishes dramatic irony and foreshadows catastrophe.

doing you a good turn, if it is to be done. And I don’t like it said

After a little further discussion as to whether it would not be better for Mrs
Tulliver to accompany them on a visit to sister Glegg, Mrs Pullet, observing
that it was tea-time, turned to reach from a drawer a delicate damask napkin,
which she pinned before her in the fashion of an apron. The door did, in fact,
soon open, but instead of the tea-tray, Sally introduced an object so startling
that both Mrs Pullet and Mrs Tulliver gave a scream, causing uncle Pullet to
swallow his lozenge—for the fifth time in his life, as he afterward
noted.

enrichment.interest_rationale: The arrival of a startling object instead of tea; cliffhanger ending with comic effect (Uncle Pullet swallowing his lozenge) that builds suspense for the chapter's conclusion.
enrichment.summary: As tea-time approaches, both Mrs Pullet and Mrs Tulliver are startled by Sally's introduction of a startling object instead of the expected tea-tray; Uncle Pullet chokes on his lozenge in surprise.
